parties:
Santipada Datta & others ----- Appellants
Vs.
Satish Chandra Das and & others ----- Respondents
book_ref: 54 DLR (AD) 173,22 BLD (AD) 246,24 BLD (AD) 43,12 BLT (AD) 27,2 ADC 211,4 ADC 844,7 MLR (AD) 249
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: This appeal by leave was to consider the submission that the High Court Division misdirected itself in holding that both the Courts below found that the plaintiff did not acquire title by adverse possession in that it was not noticed that the material evidence in that behalf was overlooked by both the Courts inasmuch as the same mistake was committed by the learned Judge himself and it was wrongly held that the elements constituting adverse possession are lacking in the case. The evidence of defendant No.1 DW 1 who was examined on commission and the only witness for the defendants if considered along with other evidence and circumstances unmistakably prove the plaintiffs possession for more than 12 years which was adverse to the admitted owner and as such, the plaintiff is entitled to a declaration of title on the basis of adverse possession. 

 2. The plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title to the suit land by purchase or adverse possession and further that the order dated 6-2-1989 of the Additional Deputy Commissioner, Comilla declaring the suit land as enemy property is illegal and inoperative. 

 3. The appellant instituted the suit stating, inter alia. that the suit land originally belonged to one Raj Lakshmi Devi, who granted settlement by a registered patta dated 29-4-1903 to one Mohesh Chandra Bhattacharjee; that on the death of the said Mahesh Chandra his wife Kala Kamini Devi and his two sons, Bidhu Bhusan and Narendra Bhattacharjee, sold the same to defendant No.1 by a kabala dated 5- 2-1940 for Taka 2,500.00 and handed over possession thereof to him; that while in possession, defendant No.1 who was in urgent need for going to Calcutta sold the suit land to the appellant for Taka 5001.00 and granted a receipt therefore on 14-2-1949; that at the time of appellant's purchase there was three huts on the suit land which were in possession of the tenants and the appellant had been possessing the suit land upon realising rents from the tenants openly and peacefully over the statutory period of 12 years to the knowledge of all concerned; that one BP Mazumder filed Miscellaneous Case No. 201 of 1964-65 in the Court of SDO, Chandpur for declaring the suit property as enemy property but the said case was rejected by order dated 23-8-1965; that thereafter one Sisir Das filed another petition on 10-9-1965 which was also dismissed on contest on 9-6-1966; then Sisir Das filed another application on 16-6-1966 which was sent to SDM for disposal who upon hearing the matter by his order dated 24-2-1967 directed the Tahsilder not to realise any rent from the tenants that against the said order Miscellaneous Case No. 9 of 1967-68 was started in the Court of ADC, Comilla who by order dated 6-3-1969 illegally declared the suit property as enemy property; that the plaintiff by virtue of his purchase and also because of his long possession over the statutory period has acquired lawful right, title and interest in the suit land and hence the suit. 

 6. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel, submits that the High Court Division as well as the Courts below misread the evidence on record and wrongly held that elements constituting adverse possession are lacking in the case and dismissed the revisional application upon an illegal view that the plaintiff did not acquire title by adverse possession inasmuch as the evidence of defendant No.1 who was examined on commission as DW 1 and the evidence of DW 1, if considered along with other evidence on record, unmistakably prove adverse possession of plaintiff for over 12 years and the High Court Division was therefore wrong in dismissing the revisional application in agreeing with the Courts below that the plaintiff did not acquire title by adverse possession. 

 The plaintiff accordingly led evidence as to the acquisition of title by adverse possession through PWs 1 and 2. The defendant though adduced one witness i.e, Tahshildar, who could not assail any of the assertions of the plaintiff but admitted that the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land and that the plaintiff and the tenants of original owner Satish have been in possession of the suit land by constructing houses thereof and that the suit land has not been leased out to anybody treating the same as vested property. The trial Court, however, simply treating the suit to be of declaration of title with prayer for confirmation of possession and without considering the evidence on record held that the plaintiff has collusively with the defendant No. 1 filed Ext. 1 to create his adverse title over adverse possession of the suit land and Satish lived in India for more than 30 years and, as such, the suit property was legally declared as the enemy property. 

 8. The Court of appeal below, however, on consideration of the evidence on record arrived at a finding that though the appellant could not prove his title on the basis of patta from the original owner Satish as there is no legal document conferring the title of the plaintiff but the plaintiff have been able to prove their possession over a period of 12 years thereby acquiring an indefeasible title by way of adverse possession. The defendant Satish while examining on commission as DW 2 has admitted the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land. But held that the plaintiff has intelligently created the papers for acquiring the suit land and, as such, relying on the Dhakhila the possession of the plaintiff would not be supported as accordingly dismissed the appeal. 

 10. Thus when there is an invalid transfer in favour of a person and he holds possession of the property transferred as transferee, his possession is in his own right and adverse to the transferee. If he continues in possession of immoveable property for more than twelve years he will acquire an in-defeasible title. 

 "As to the second and the most vital aspect of the case, namely, title by adverse possession, a few facts may not be lost sight of. Adverse possession implies that it had commenced in wrong and is maintained against right. The plaintiff has claimed to have his entry into the disputed land under an agreement of purchase with defendant No. 1 who had no title thereto as found by the trial Court and which finding was not reversed by the appellate Court. In such a case when the plaintiff after getting into possessing retains the same with clean animus that he has become the absolute owner of the property in complete negation of any right or title of the true owner thereof ie defendant No. 2, his enjoyment would be solely in assertion of hostile title." 

 12. In the case of Abdul Kader vs Noor Mohammad 36 DLR (AD) 261 this Court quoted with approval the following observation of Sanderson CJ that: "the term adverse possession implies that the person against whom adverse possession is exercised is a person who is entitled to demand possession at the moment adverse possession begins." 

 13. In the case of Ejaz Ali Qidwai vs Special Manager; Court of wards, Bulrampur Estate AIR 1935 PC 53 the principle of adverse possession was laid when "a person who bases his title on adverse possession by clear and unequivocal evidence that his possession was hostile to the real owner and amounted to a denial of his title to the property claimed." 

 14. In the case of Hafiz Mohammad Fateh Nasib vs Sir Swamp Chandra Hukum Chand (1947) 52 CWN 382 the list to be applied in respect of adverse possession has been spelt out as "The Correct test to be applied in a case of this nature is, whether the claimant exercised such domain over the property as to justify the inference that he was in possession of the whole. It is not necessary for him to prove that he was in physical possession of every square inch." Thus possession under a mistaken or invalid title is as effective as that of a trespasser and If sufficient in length of time and continuity gives the holder a title. 

 17. From the evidence we find that the plaintiff has categorically deposed that he has been in possession on the basis of lease granted through receipt and that the lease has been supported by the receipt issued at a time when the plaintiff was present and the same has been supported by PW 2. Defendant No. 1 examined on commission stated that he has transferred the suit land in favour of the plaintiff on the basis of receipt which was written in presence of the witnesses and delivered the huts to the plaintiff on receipt of the consideration money and duly signed the receipt evidencing receipt of the amount on 14-2-49. Since the receipt is not a deed of title it could not confer title to the plaintiff under the provision of section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act but the uninterrupted adverse and hostile possession of the plaintiff over a period of 12 years from the date of 14 February 1949 up to 1961 ie., the period prior of alleged declaration of property as enemy property, the plaintiff has acquired title by adverse possession.

caseno: Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 226 of 2000
parties:
Lt. Gen. (Rtd) Hussain Muhammad Ershad ------ petitioner
-Versus-
The State ------ respondent
full_judgment:
The order of the former President H.M. Ershad was forwarded to Chairman, RAJUK who on 12.9.89 allotted the aforesaid lands in groups at the rate of Tk. 1,93,550/- per katha in favour of accused Abdus Sukur Prodhan, Md. Sikander Hussain, Abdul Wadud Khan, Abraham Purification, Md. Shafiqul Islam, Md. Jahangir Alam, Md. Khalilur Rahman, Mrs. Lovely Begum, Md. Nowab Miah, Md. Abu Hanif, Shahinoor Islam, Mosammat Aftara Begum and one Sadek Hossain dividing the plot into four plots i.e. No. 49, 49A, 49B and 49C. Plot No. 49 with an area of 12 Kathas was allotted to accused Shahinoor Islam, Aftara Begum and one Sadeque Hussain at a total price of Tk. 23,22,600/-. The money was deposited on 18.9.89 and possession of the land was delivered on 19.9.89 in favour of the lessees. The lease deed was registered on 21.10.89 and on the very next day i.e. 22.10.89 the lessees sought permission of the RAJUK to transfer plot No. 49 in favour Of JPI, for a total consideration of Tk. 33,00,000/-. On 25.10.89 RAJUK accorded permission for transfer. The deed was registered on 2.11.89 in favour of the JPL. It is alleged that Md. Sadeque Hussain was residing abroad at the relevant time and accused Amjadul Haque forged signature of Sadeque Hossain on the lease deed and did everything in the name of the said absentee Sadeque Hussain by false impersonation including forging signature in the deed of sale in favour of JPL. It is the further case of the prosecution that although in the transfer deed the total price was shown as Tk. 33,00,000/-. but Shahinoor Islam, Aftara Begum and Amjadul Haque did not receive any money from JPI, and they only received Tk. 1,63,000/- from Abdus Sukur Prodhan. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dhaka by his Memo dated 8.10.89 informed the RAJUK that none of the above mentioned allottees were originally affected persons. In order to get allotment the allottee must be an original affected person. It is clear from the letter of the A.D.C. (Revenue) Dhaka dated 8.10.89 that none of the applicants was original affected person. The former President without verifying the truth of the statements and without taking steps for such verification passed order for giving allotment to those persons directly which was illegal. It was further alleged that no transfer could be made without construction on the land, but in this case the impediment was overcame by RAJUK by amending paragraph 20 of the Standard Lease Deed on 22.10.89. It was alleged that these allotment were made with the ulterior motive to give the land to JPL of which accused Rawshan Ara Begum was the Chairperson and accused Abdus Sattar former Minister and Chief Whip was a Director. It was alleged that the former President H.M. Ershad and M.M. Rahmat Ullah in collusion with each other dishonestly and fraudulently with a malafide intention helped the 13 accused-applicants to get illegally the lease of the land in their favour and then helped JPL and its Directors to get 12 kathas of land of plot No. 49 at a negligible sum causing loss to RAJUK to the sum of Tk. 5,48,70,900/- to obtain pecuniary advantage for themselves or for others. All other accused abated illegally in collusion with each other to obtain pecuniary advantages. 

 8. The defence of other accused persons is that they are affected persons and as such they applied to get the land requisitioned by DIT in L.A. Case No. 13 of 1962-63. On various dates in 1985 the petitioners along with others purchased some lands by registered sale deeds from the original owners with all their right, title and interest in the said land. On 4.12.85 the said land was mutated in the name of the petitioners along with others and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Land Administration) recorded the names of the petitioners as awardees in L.A. Case No. 13 of 1962-63 in place of the original owners. By virtue of the purchase and mutation the petitioners entered into the position of the original owners as far as to the right, title and interest of the land in question is concerned. Finally one day, when the former President went to offer Jumma Prayer at Ambar Shah Mosque the local people including the petitioners urged the then President to return the land to the petitioners as affected persons and on hearing them the former President asked them to file a formal representation. Accordingly on 26.8.89 the petitioners along with others submitted an application addressing to the then present and as such the President asked the RAJUK on 28.8.89 to allot the land to the petitioners as affected persons and as highest bidders in auction at the auction price. 

 15. The entire case started on the basis of an application filed by co-accused Abdus Sukur Prodhan and other accused wherein they stated that they are the highest bidder on auction on 5.9.85 and they are also affected persons due to requisition of their land in L.A. Case No. 13/62-63. On this application the order, Ext. 18 was passed on 28.8.89 by former President H.M. Ershad directing for allotting land to the applicants. We shall have to see first as to whether the applicant co-accused Abdus Sukur Prodhan and others are really affected persons due to the requisition of the land in L.A. Case No. 13/62-63. P.W.7 Mosleuddin Mia, Bench Assistant of Land Acquisition officer (RAJUK Branch) of Dhaka Colloctorate deposed that the part file of L.A. Case No. 13/62-63 was seized by the Police which has been marked as Ext. 22. P.W. 8 Md. Shamsul Haque Mia Kanungo of L.A. Branch deposed that in the file of L.A. Case No. 13/62-63 the name of co-accused Abdus Sukur Prodhan and 14 others are entered in the list of awardees. According to this witness Abdus Sukur Prodhan filed the first petition on 28.11.85 for getting his name enlisted as an awardee in the said L.A. Case No. 13/62-63. According to this witness Abdus Sukur Prodhan purchased 115 Adjutangsha land of Plot No. 41 and 14/133 of Khatian 48, Mauja Kawran from Nitai Das Rishi who was original owner and whose land was acquired in L.A. Case No. 13/62-63. According to P.W. 8 on 4.12.85 the amendment of the award was made wherein the names of the original affected persons were mentioned. It is also noted in the L.A. Case file that the amount of compensation was paid to the original owner and Nitai Das Rishi received the compensation of Tk. 2050/-on 17.6.65 in the first installment. It is also in evidence of P.W. 8 that on 13.11.85 Abdus Sukur Prodhan filed a photo copy of Kabala alleged to have been executed by Nitai Das Rashi for 3 shatangsha land of Plot No. 42 of Kawran Bazar and his name was also substituted on 21.11.85. According to this witness on 29.5.64 Nitai Das Rishi and others (original owners) received provisional compensation of Tk. 4,140/, This witness has further testified that all other accused also filed applications in 1985 and 1986 claiming that they also purchased some portion of requisition land from original owners in L.A. Case No. 13/62-63 and on that basis got their name entered as awardees. This witness also stated that ADC Sirajul Islam gave note in Ext. 41 to Chairman RAJUK stating that the 13 persons whose names were mentioned as awardees were not original affected person in L.A. Case No. 13/62-63. This witness also stated that these lands were acquired under Town Improvement Act, 1953. He also admitted in cross-examination that some undisbursed fund was lying in connection with the said L.A. Case No. 13/62-63. Thus from the evidence of P.W. 8 and from Ext. 22 and Ext. 42, the file relating to Plot No. 49 KCA it is palpably clear that the plot in question was requisitioned under the Town Improvement Act. 1953 in L.A. Case No. 13/62-63 and the original owners received compensation soon thereafter. Accused Abdus Sukur Prodhan and others obtained kabalas in the year 1985/86 showing purchase of a very small traction of land from the original owners whose land was acquired in L.A. Case and laid their claim for the remaining part compensation money and enlisted their names as awardees. Thus it is very clear from the evidence of 8 that they knew that the land has been acquired as far back as in 1962 and knowing that the original owners received compensation the names were enlisted. They procured the sale deeds in the year 1985 and in 1986 and thereafter entered their names in place of original owners as awardees and subsequently filed the application before the former President of the Republic. In reality from the oral and documentary evidence it is found that they were not affected persons in the L.A. Case. In between 1985-86, that is, 22/23 years after requisition of the land under Town Improvement Act, 1953 these accused persons took steps for substituting their names as awardees in place of the original awardees. 

 17. P.W. 10 Abdur Rahman Bhuiya, Director of Estates, RAJUK stated that KCA was acquired in L.A. Case No. 13/62-63 through Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka. He further deposed from the file, Ext. 42 that Plot Nos. 49 and 49A were put on auction on 5.9.85 wherein Abdus Sukur Prodhan and three others participated in auction of Plot No. 49. One Golam Kibria and three others participated in auction of Plot No. 49A. The bid being inadequate the auction was cancelled. According to this witness the minimum price per Bigha was mentioned at Tk. 3 crores in the note sheet and the note was written by Mr. Humayon Khadem the then Director Land and Estate. This witness also testified that Abdus Sukur Prodhan and others filed Title Suit No. 4 of 1989. He also proved the recommendation of the President in the application of 13 accused persons as Ext. 18. According to this witness the application was filed by Abdus Sukur Prodhan on 26.8.89 before the President who gave allotment order on 28.8.89. This witness received that application on 29.8.89 from Rahmatullah, Chairman, RAJUK. This witness further stated that the file was always kept with the Chairman himself. According to this witness as per note allotment letters were prepared and those were distributed to the accused persons. He also testified that Plot Nos. 49 and 49A were allotted to four groups dividing the same into 4 plots that is Plot Nos. 49. 49A, 49B and 49C, Plot No. 49 with an area of 12 katha was allotted to Shahinoor Islam, Sadek Hossain and Aftara Begum. Plot No. 49A with an area of 10 katha was allotted to Jahangir Alam, Shafiqul Islam and Abrahyam Purification. Plot No. 49B with an area of 10 katha was allotted to Abu Hanif. Nawab Miah, Lovely Begum and Khalilur Rahman Plot No. 49C with an area of 10 katha was allotted to Abdul Wadud Khan, Abdus Sukur Prodhan. Sekander Hossain Khan, This witness further stated that in auction notice dated 19.1.89 the minimum price of land per bigha was fixed Tk. 3 crores. At the rate of 3 crores per bigha the value of 2 bighas 1 katha land was Tk. 6,50,00,000/-. But the lease money of the said land was realised only Tk. 79,35,550/- and as such RAJUK sustained loss of Tk. 5,70,00,000/-. In cross examination this witness stated that accused Abdus Sukur Prodhan and others were not original affected persons in the said L.A. Case, but during the period from 1985/87 Sukur Prodhan and others got their names enlisted in the award on the plea of purchase from the original owner whose land was acquired. P.W. 16 Syed Mokbul Ahmed authorized officer of RAJUK proved the plan of multistoried building of 49 KCA. According to this witness on 17.12.89 Rawshan Ara Begum (wife of H.M. Ershad) filed an application in a printed form for approval of plan for construction of a 15 storied building at Plot No. 49 KCA. Clearance certificate was given on 19.12.89. He further testified that Rowshan Ara Begum mentioned her address at 24, Amin Bagh, Shantinagar, Dhaka. P.W. 20 Md. Shahidur Rahman, Dealing Assistant of Estate Section, RAJUK testified that he saw the file, Ext 42 at the meeting room. According to this witness the file was kept in personal custody of co-accused Chairman Mr. Rahmatullah. P.W. 21 Abu Baker Sk. Assistant Director, RAJUK deposed that the co-accused kept the file, Ext. 42 in his custody. P.W. 22 Syed Abbasuddin, Law Superintendent of RAJUK deposed that Ext. 42 was with the Chairman although. This witness also corroborated witness P.W. 20 on material particulars. P.W. 32 Lt. Col. (Rtd) Nurul Hoque, Member, Land and Estate, RAJUK deposed that Ext. 42, 47, 48, 49 and 50 are the files of land and Estate Department of RAJUK which were handed over to him by Rahmatullah at the time of his departure from the post of Chairman. P.W. 34 Md. Humaun Khadem, Member, Planning and Development deposed that, Ext. 42 is the file relating to Plot No. 49 of KCA. He admitted that there was no approval of allotment of Plot Nos. 49 and 49A of the RAJUK. He further stated that Plot No. 49, 49A, 49B, and 49C were allotted in the year 1989 and those were not allotted by RAJUK. He further stated that the permission for transferring the land in favour of JPL was given by the Chairman RAJUK. RAJUK did not accord permission for transfer in favour of JPL. 

 18. From an analysis of the above evidence of the officers of RAJUK it is found that Plot Nos. 49 and 49A were acquired in land acquisition case as far back as in 1962. The bid that was submitted by Abdus Sukur Prodhan and others in respect of those plots as affected persons though highest was not accepted being low. From the evidence it is also found that Abdus Sukur Prodhan and others filed Title Suit No. 76 of 1987 and also got status quo in that suit. From the evidence of officials of RAJUK as discussed above it is also found that H.M. Ershad passed order for allotment of land in favour of accused Abdus Sukur Prodhan and others as per the endorsement Ext. 18. From the evidence it further appears that the co-accused enlisted their names as awardees only in 1985-87. These witnesses also denied the suggestion that RAJUK did not sustain any loss for allotment of Plot No. 49 and 49A of KCA. It also appears from the evidence of those witnesses as discussed above that the file was mostly kept in custody of Chairman, RAJUK. From the evidence of P.W. 34 it also appears that no approval was given for allotment of Plot Nos. 49 and 49A by RAJUK. It also appears from the discussion of the evidence that in the previous auction notice of Plot No. 49 and 49A minimum price was not mentioned whereas auction for Plot No. 49 and 49A was published in the year of 1987 in which minimum price of auction was quoted Tk. 3 crores per bigha. From the evidence of P.W. 34 it also appears that the permission for transferring the land in favour of JPL was given by Chairman, RAJUK. It also further appears that the RAJUK did not accord permission for transferring the land in favour of JPL.

parties:
Halima Jaman and other ------ Petitioner
vs.
Government of Bangladesh ------ Respondent
full_judgment: 2. Original plaintiff Asaduzzaman filed Title Suit No. 101 of 1973 of the 4th court of learned Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, (subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 107 of 1988 of the 3rd Court of learned Subordinate Judge, Dhaka) against defendant No. 1 A Satter Solaiman for specific performance of contract. Plaintiff Asaduzzaman died on 8-12-1991 (after dismissal of the suit on 9-6-1990). The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that defendant No. l A. Satter Solaiman, admittedly a non-Bengali national, executed an agreement on 14-10-1971 for sale of the suit property to the plaintiff at a consideration of taka one lac and bainapatra (Ext. 1) was executed by A Satter Solaiman on 14-10-1971 on receipt of Taka 75,000.00 as earnest money. It was stipulated that A Sattar Solaiman would execute and register the sale deed in favour of plaintiff Asaduzzaman. It is the case of the plaintiff that A Satter Solaiman delivered possession of the property in his favour on 14-10-1971. A deed of sale having not been executed and registered by A Satter Solaiman, the plaintiff was obliged to file the suit for specific performance of contract. In the written statements defendant No.2 Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and defendant No.3 Giasuddin Ahmed, claiming to be a lessee from the Government, denied the existence of any agreement for sale of the suit property contending that A Satter Solaiman left the then East Pakistan long before execution of the alleged agreement for sale of the suit property. The written statements claimed that the agreement for sale was a forged and fabricated document created for filing a suit for specific performance of contract. Subsequently the written statement of defendant No 1 A Salter Solaiman was struck off by the court, because the power of Attorney of the defendant had not been validated in Bangladesh and the written statement of defendant No.3 was also struck off on 24-6-1975 on the expiry of his lease. Before the trial Court as many as two witnesses were examined by the plaintiff as against none by the defendant. The trial Court dismissed the suit for failure of the plaintiff to prove due execution of the bainapatra and the Judgment and decree of the court below was upheld by a Division Bench of this court in First Appeal No. 184 of 1990. The trial Court held that the plaintiff could not prove writing of the documentby the scribe and that the plaintiff also did not examine the two attesting witnesses, Abdul Karim and Abdul Latif, and further that it was hardly believable that PW 1 Halima Jaman, wife of Asaduzzaman, and PW 2 Md Shajahan, a cousin of PW 1 were present in the house of defendant No. 1 at the time of execution of the document inasmuch as there was no attestation of the said agreement by these two witnesses. In other words, the suit was dismissed by the trial Court and the Judgment was upheld by a Division Bench of this court on the failure of the plaintiff to prove due execution of the deed of agreement. The present application under Order 47, rule 1 of the CPC for review of the Judgment passed in First Appeal No. 184 of 1990 has been submitted mainly on the ground of death of A Satter Solaiman on 10-12-1973. The suit was dismissed by the trial Court on 9-6-1990 and the First Appeal against the Judgment and decree of dismissal was dismissed on 12-4-1994.

parties:
Chittagong Development Authority, represented by its Chairman and others ------ Petitioner
Vs. 
Rokeya Anwar and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
2. Opposite Party No. 1 as plaintiff instituted a suit in the Court of the Assistant Judge, 2nd Court, Chittagong, being Other Suit No. 96 of 1978, praying for declaration of title and mandatory injunction alleging, inter alia, that suit plot No. 489 in Agrabad Residential Area, Chittagong was settled with Mofazal Ahmed and Fazal Hoque, defendant Nos. 7 and 8 respectively and they owned and possessed the same. Subsequently on taking permission from the Chittagong Development Authority (CDA) defendant Nos. 7 and 8 transferred the suit land to plaintiff No. 1 and in the lease deed in question 4.666 kathas of land was mentioned. In course of time the plaintiff constructed pucca buildings in the said premises and since then she has been residing therein. It has been further contended that at the time of construction of the house it was detected that the suit land actually comprises more than 4.666 kathas as mentioned in the deed of lease, following which the plaintiff filed an application before the CDA for granting her lease of the excess land in terms of the conditions embodied in the deed of agreement but the CDA instead of allowing the said prayer for lease of the excess land directed the plaintiff by letter dated 27-11-88 to surrender the excess land to the CDA and this necessitated the filing of the suit. 

 3. Defendant Nos. 1-5 contested the suit by filing written statements denying the material allegations of the plaint and contended, inter alia, that suit plot No. 489 with an area of 4.696 kathas only was leased out to the vendors of the plaintiff and the area of the land settled was specifically mentioned in the lease deed as 4.696 kathas of land and, as such, the plaintiff''s claim for more than 4.696 kathas of land cannot be entertained. It was further contended that the quantum of land allotted to the settle was clearly and specifically mentioned in the lease deed in terms of the lease agreement and the site-map and the sketch-map appended thereto are mere indications for the purpose of identification of the land settled and these by no means indicate the actual quantum of land demised. It was further contended that the plaintiff illegally encroached upon the land of schedule No. 2 to the plaint, in which she has no title and interest. Since the suit land as described in Schedule No. 2 to the plaint is admittedly the land of the Chittagong Development Authority, which fact has not been denied by the plaintiff or her predecessors-in-interest, the plaintiff cannot claim this excess land as a matter of right and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 3) Whether the plaintiff has any title, interest and possession in the suit property? and 

 4) To what relief, if any, the plaintiff is entitled to? 

 5. At the trial the plaintiff examined two witnesses and the contesting defendant examined four witnesses and exhibited documents in support of their respective cases. The learned Assistant Judge by the impugned judgment dated 31-1-89 decreed the suit and directed defendant Nos. 1-5 for giving settlement of the land of Schedule 2 to the plaint to the plaintiff within 60 days of the decree. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree the defendant petitioners took an appeal before the District Judge, Chittagong, who was pleased by the impugned judgment dated 15-3-93 to dismiss the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. It is to be noted in this connection that the trial Court while decreeing the suit did not declare the plaintiff''s title in the suit land, which tantamount to rejection of the plaintiff's prayer for declaration of her title in the suit land. It appears from the record that the plaintiff did not prefer any cross-objection against it after defendant-petitioners preferred Other Class Appeal No. 109 of 1989 before the District Judge, Chittagong and, as such, the plaintiff is deemed to have accepted the said refusal to declare her title in the suit land gracefully. 

 7. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioners, submits that the learned Courts below erred in law in decreeing the suit without noticing and considering that the suit was clearly barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and the same has occasioned failure of justice. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that the learned Courts below seriously erred in law in holding that the boundaries of the suit land shall prevail over the area of the land mentioned in the lease agreement Ext. 2 and Ext. A, which clearly show that only 4.96 kathas of land in suit plot No. 489 was settled with the allotees, who are the vendors of the present plaintiff, and possession of the said land was made over to them and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr Bhuiyan further submits that in the face of the admitted fact that 4.966 kathas of land in suit plot No. 489 was settled with the plaintiff by lease agreement Ext. 2, and the plaintiff prayed for settlement of lease of the excess amount of land measuring 4.80 square feet and for a declaration of title over the excess amount of land than originally settled, the suit for declaration of title and permanent injunction relating to the said excess land is not contemplated in law and, as such, the learned Courts below misdirected themselves to decree the suit on an erroneous view of law and the same has occasioned failure of justice. Mr Bhuiyan further submits that the lay-out plan, site-map, etc. merely indicate the location and identification of the suit land and not the quantum of land settled with the allottees, which was specifically mentioned in the lease deed as 4.966 kathas of land only, and the plaintiff accepted the same and acted upon the same taking it to be so, as has been specifically admitted in paragraph 9 of the plaint, and consequently, the plaintiffs claim of title in the excess land is not contemplated in law and the learned Courts below clearly erred in law in decreeing the suit completely ignoring the scope of the suit and the same has occasioned failure of justice. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that in view of the admitted fact that no vested right was created in favour of the plaintiff for getting settlement of Schedule 2 land and there was no corresponding legal obligation on the part of the CDA to grant lease of the said land in favour of the plaintiff, the learned Courts below erred in law in decreeing the suit completely ignoring this material aspect of the case and the law bearing on the subject and the same has occasioned failure of justice. 

 8. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite party, on the other hand, submits that the learned Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff is entitled to get settlement of Schedule 2 land and the impugned judgment thus being concluded by concurrent findings of fact is not to be interfered with by this Court exercising power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Khondker further submits that although the trial Court and, as a matter of fact, the appellate Court did not declare the plaintiff's title in the suit land, nevertheless there was a prayer for declaration of plaintiff''s title in the suit land and, as such, in the facts and circumstance of the case and the evidence on record, the plaintiff''s title in the suit land can be declared by this Court exercising revisional power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Khondker further submits that since the plaintiff was successful in proving her case the suit has rightly been decreed and the said decree cannot be interfered with in revision as it has not occasioned any failure of justice. 

 11. While disposing of the appeal the learned Additional District Judge also failed to discuss and consider any evidence of the 6 witnesses examined by the contending parties and dismissed the appeal on the finding that the plaintiff being in possession of Schedule 2 land as an integral part of Schedule 1 land has become the rightful owner of the scheduled land and, as such, she was entitled to get lease of Schedule 2 land on payment of proportionate premium to the CDA. The learned Additional District Judge further held that the boundary of the suit land will prevail over the area mentioned in the lease deed Ext. 2. From the impugned judgments it appears that neither the trial Court nor the appellate Court took the pains of discussing and considering the material evidence of the 6 witnesses examined by the contending parties. 

 13. The moot question in this case is as to whether the plaintiff has any vested legal right in claiming the settlement of Schedule 2 land and whether the defendant CDA was under any legal obligation to grant lease of the excess land contained in Schedule 2 of the plaint in favour of the plaintiff. In the absence of any vested legal right on the part of the plaintiff and a corresponding legal obligation on the part of the CDA to grant lease of the excess land in favour of the plaintiff, the plaintiff's claim for settlement cannot be entertained. Neither the trial Court nor the lower appellate Court appeal's to have addressed itself to this vital question nor has it drawn any conclusion on it on the basis of the evidence on record. Nowhere in the impugned judgments it is found that the learned Courts below held that the plaintiff is entitled to get settlement of the suit land as of right and the CDA is under a legal obligation to make such settlement. The plaintiff did not make out any case of adverse possession, establishing any claim for life. 

 14. In paragraph No. 9 of the plaint it has been specifically mentioned that the plaintiff bona fide believed that she took the settlement of only 4.999 kathas of land from the CDA and acting on the said premises she owned and possessed the suit land but while taking actual measurement of the suit land at the time of construction of her house it was detected that the suit land actually measured 5.666 kathas and not 4.966 kathas as mentioned in the lease deed. In the facts and circumstances of the case the trial Court as well as the appellate Court rightly did not find plaintiff's title in the suit land described in Schedule 2 of the plaint. 

 15. Admittedly, the CDA is the owner of Schedule 2 land, as such, in the absence of a definite proof of acquisition of title or interest by the plaintiff in Schedule 2 land and a corresponding legal obligation on the part of the CDA to grant lease of the Schedule 2 land to the plaintiff, there cannot be any direction by the Court upon the CDA to grant lease of the excess land in favour of the plaintiff. In the frame of the suit the prayer for a direction upon the defendant CDA to grant lease of Schedule 2 land to the plaintiff appears to be barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The Courts below seriously erred in law in decreeing the suit on a casual view of the matter and without considering this vital legal question and the law bearing on the subject and the same has occasioned failure of justice. 

 18. In this case the plaintiff filed the suit praying for getting lease of Schedule 2 land from the CDA. Subsequently, of course, the plaint was amended adding a prayer for declaration of title. Nowhere from the record it is found as to how the plaintiff acquired title in Schedule 2 land. It has been clearly admitted in paragraph No. 9 of the plaint that the plaintiff got settlement of 4.999 kathas of land on the basis of lease deed Ext. 2 and she acted on the same premises bona fide believing that the acquired title and interest in that quantum of land only and it never occurred to her that she got interest in 5.666 kathas of land till before the physical measurement of the suit land at the time of construction of her house thereon. It is thus evident that the additional 4.80 sqft of land was clearly beyond the contemplation and comprehension of the contending parties while concluding the lease deed Ext. 2. This excess land measuring 4.80 square feet thus clearly falls outside the purview of the lease agreement in question and consequently, the plaintiff cannot claim the same as a matter of right and the defendant CDA cannot be compelled to give settlement of the same to the plaintiff. It is thus crystal clear that the plaintiff did not acquire any title in Schedule 2 land. The only material question that remained for consideration by the Courts was whether the plaintiffs claim for getting lease of excess land contained in Schedule 2 of the plaint could be entertained and a direction from the Court to the CDA for granting such lease of the same in favour of the plaintiff could lawfully be made. Since I have already found that there is nothing on record to prove that the plaintiff has acquired any right and title in Schedule 2 land admittedly the CDA is the owner of Schedule 2 land, and there being no corresponding legal obligation on the part of the CDA to grant lease of the same to the plaintiff, the Court cannot give a mandate compelling the defendant CDA to grant lease of the suit land to the plaintiff. Such a direction could be given only if a clear case was made out in favour of the plaintiff establishing a definite legal right for her for the enforcement of which the Court could come to her rescue in a properly constituted suit for Specific Performance of Contract. But, in the instant case, in the light of the case made out in the plaint and the evidence adduced at the trial I do not find any such legal right in favour of the plaintiff and a corresponding legal obligation on the part of the defendant CDA for granting lease of the Schedule 2 land to the plaintiff and, as such, the impugned decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge and subsequently affirmed by the learned appellate Court cannot be sustained in law. The impugned judgment is thus found to be neither legal nor proper and the same has occasioned failure of justice. The concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the learned Courts below are not supported by the evidence on record and the law bearing on the subject and, as such, the same are not sustainable. For the reasons stated above the submissions made by the learned Counsel for the petitioners are sustained and those made by the learned Counsel for the opposite party are repelled. 

 19. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Chittagong in Title Appeal. No. 109 of 1989 affirming the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Sadar, Chittagong in Other Suit No. 96 of 1978 are set aside and Other Suit No. 96 of 1978 of the 2nd Court of the Assistant Judge, Chittagong is hereby dismissed.

parties:
Asma Begum ------ Petitioner
Vs. 
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary Ministry of Works Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
31. The petitioner, although, claimed to have purchased the disputed property in the year 1968, did not file the original document of title that is the Standard Agreement for Allotment of House. The petitioner failed to show that she got her name mutated with the Housing Estate and paid rent. The petitioner did not file Non-option certificate and also the Nationality certificate from the competent authority. In the absence of those papers, it is difficult on our part to accept the contention that the petitioner, since the Liberation of Bangladesh, all along had been in Bangladesh and her whereabouts were known. 

 41. It remains now to consider the submissions advanced before us on behalf of the respondent that in view of the violation of clause 3 of the original Agreement For Allotment of House, the deed of conveyance of the petitioner became invalid. We do not find any substance in the said submission. Annexure-B(1) is a document showing full payment of Taka 2700.00 to the erstwhile Government of East Pakistan. It appears that the lessee Abdul Kader Mullick before execution and registration of the deed of conveyance paid the entire consideration money of Taka 2700.00 by way of chalan to the Administrative Officer, Housing Estate and the lessee Abdul Kader Mullick being the full owner of the house property transferred the same to the petitioner.

parties:
Abdur Rouf Chowdhury (Md) and 4 others ------ Petitioners
Vs. 
Additional Deputy Commissioner (Land Acquisition) & others ------ Respondents

Nilufa Begum ----- Appellant
Vs.
Md. Atash Ali and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Sirajul Islam J: This appeal by the plaintiff is directed against the judgment and decree dated 21-4-1993 and 26-4-1993 passed by Subordinate Judge 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 133 of 1987 dismissing the plaintiff's suit on the preliminary issue of maintainability. 

 2. The appellant Mst. Nilufa Begum as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 133 of 1987 in the court of Subordinate Judge 1st Court, Dhaka against the defendant Md. Atash Ali and others for a declaration of plaintiff's right, title and interest in the suit land by treating the impugned final decree dated 16-6-1980 passed in Title Suit No.92 of 1966 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka as fraudulent, illegal, nullity and not binding upon the plaintiff. The plaintiff's case, in short, is that the piece and parcels of land measuring 0.53 decimals in different plots described in the schedule to the plaint along with other lands originally belonged to one Sk. Emminat who while owning and possessing the same died leaving behind his only son Sk. Himmat as his sole heir to inherit the suit land. That the plaintiff's father Sekandar Ali Bepari purchased the suit land from some lineal descendants of Sk. Himmat vide registered kabala dated 7-10-63. One Suburjan Bibi and 2 others filed Title Suit No. 92 of 1966 for partition of the suit land and other land impleading the plaintiff's father Sk. Sekandar Ali Bepari as defendant No. 42. Defendant contested Title Suit No. 92 of 1966 in the court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court; Dhaka by filing a written statement claiming his share as a co-sharer in the suit land by purchase. Considering the facts, circumstances and the evidence of the case, the learned Subordinate Judge, decreed the Title Suit No. 92 of 1966 on contest against contesting defendant No. 42 Sekandar Ali Bepari and ex parte against the rest in the preliminary form by his judgment and decree dated 23-11-1968. 

 3. Against that judgment and decree of the Title Suit No. 92 of 1966 that Sekandar Ali Bepari (defendant r 42), the father of the present plaintiff, preferred first appeal No. 95 of 1969 in this court. During the pendency of the appeal in this court, the sole appellant Sekandar Ali died on 19-10-77. Thereafter, the heirs of Sekandar Ali appeared by power and filed an application for their substitution in place of their deceased predecessor Sekandar Ali and accordingly, they were substituted by order dated 12-1-1978 and thus they proceeded with the appeal. Ultimately, after hearing both the parties, the first Appeal No.95 of 1969 was dismissed by judgment dated 20-4-1979. After disposal of the appeal, record of Title Suit No.92 of 1966 went back to the trial Court and then the learned Subordinate Judge through usual process made the preliminary decree final by judgment and decree dated 16-6-1980. 

 4. Thereafter the present plaintiff Nilufa Begum filed the present Title Suit No. 133 of 1987 on 19-3-1987 and her main allegation in the plaint is that after the death of her father (defendant No. 42 of title Suit No. 92 of 1966) his heirs were substituted by the plaintiff showing this Nilufa Begum as major defendant No. 42(n) in spite of her being a minor at that time and that was done fraudulently at the instance of her step brother Habibur Rahman outside the knowledge of the plaintiff and of her mother and natural guardian who is still alive. That the plaintiff Nilufa Begum was not properly represented in that partition suit and hence the final decree passed on 16-6-1980 in that partition suit is a nullity and not binding upon the plaintiff. The plaintiff's further case is that the final decree was obtained against some dead persons also and that the decree is a nullity in that sense also. The plaintiff has been in possession of the suit land and that defendants are quite strangers in respect of the suit land. Although writ of delivery of possession in the final decree was issued but it was not actually executed on the spot The defendant has no right, title or possession in the suit land. The plaintiff had her possession on the suit land. The decree passed against her during her minority is not binding against the plaintiff. That the decree has clouded the plaintiffs title to the suit land and hence the plaintiff is now constrained to file the present suit No. 133 of 1987 for declaration as aforesaid. 

 5. During the proceeding of the suit, the defendants 1, 2, 4-17 filed an application under Order 7 rule 11 CPC for rejecting the plaint but that the learned Subordinate Judge had rejected that application for rejection of the plaint vide order dated 21-4-1987. Against that order, the defendant moved this court in Civil Revision No. 466 of 1987 and the Rule was discharged vide this Court's order dated 8-11-1990. Thereafter, the Title Suit No. 133 of 1987 was proceeding in the trial Court and during this period, the defendant Nos. 1-12 filed a further application under Order 14 rule 2 read with Order 15 rule 3(1, 2) CPC on 1-9-91 praying for framing an issue of maintainability and for dismissing the suit as being not maintainable in this form and accordingly, an issue of maintainability appears to have been framed by order dated 22-1-1992. Then after several adjournments this petition and the issue of maintainability was ultimately heard and disposed of by the learned Subordinate Judge on 21-4-1993. After hearing both the parties and considering the facts and circumstances relevant to the case, the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the defendant's application filed under Order 14 rule 2 read with Order 15 rule 3(1,2) CPC and dismissed the plaintiff's suit on the issue of maintainability vide his judgment and decree dated 21-4-1993 and 26-4-1993 respectively. 

 10. Next point urged by Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-appellant, is that Sekandar Ali Bepari, the father of Nilufa Begum, died during the pendency of the First Appeal No. 95 of 1969 filed against the original preliminary decree of Title Suit No. 92 of 1966 and that while substituting the heirs of deceased Sekandar Ali (defendant 42 of Title Suit No. 92 of 1966) this Nilufa Begum was shown as a major in spite of the fact that she was a minor at that time and that she was show major fraudulently at the instance of her step-brother, Habibur Rahman in collusion with the defendants and similarly, she was shown as major while substituting them in Title Suit No. 92 of 1966 at the time of making the preliminary decree final and thus the plaintiff Nilufa Begum of the present suit was not properly represented nor had she any knowledge about her substitution as a major and the final decree thus obtained in Title Suit No. 92 of 1966 is a fraudulent decree and hence this final decree in question is a nullity and is not binding against the present plaintiff Nilufa Begum. The learned Advocate argued that the learned Subordinate Judge did not discuss the facts as per statement made by the plaintiff in her plaint nor considered the papers relevant therewith and thus he came to a wrong finding that the plaintiffs suit was not maintainable and was barred by res judicata and, as such, the judgment and decree passed by the Subordinate Judge is not sustainable in law. 

 12. In the vokalatnama it appears that this Nilufa has signed her name at serial No.14 in the vokalatnama along with the name of her mother Jamila Khatun and other brothers. By a reading of the plaint as filed by Nilufa Begum in Title Suit No. 133 of 1987 it appears that not a single word has been stated about the signature of Nilufa as is there in the vokalatnama filed by all of them as heirs of their deceased father in this court. It is not stated in the plaint whether it was her signature or whether her signature was obtained by mis-representation. While his attention was drawn to this fact of the signature of Nilufa Begum along with her mother and brothers in the vokalatnama and in the application Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate for the appellant, said that the signature of Nilufa is neither denied nor affirmed. It has been simply stated in the plaint that substitution petition was made at the instance of her step-brother Habibur Rahman outside the knowledge of the plaintiff and her natural guardian mother who is still alive. But the fact remains that in this statement as made in the plaint also Nilufa did not deny her signature. On the other hand, her mother stated to be still alive has not made any statement or objection any where since the time of substitution on 12-1-1978 till to-day nor did she raise any objection in respect of this vokalatnama as filed therein. It appears that the same substitution of the some persons as per their own statement as made swearing in an affidavit in this court was made in the trial Court at the time of making the final decree. In this view of the matter, we find that the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly commented that at the time of substitution of this plaintiff Nilufa Begum along with other heirs of the deceased Sekandar Ali the plaintiffs of partition suit No. 92 of 1966 or for that matter the defendants of present Title Suit No. 133 of 1987 had no role to play. Therefore, the question of fraud by the defendants of the present suit does not arise. It was their own application on which the substitution was made. We fully agree with this observation as made by the learned Subordinate Judge while disposing of the plaintiffs Title Suit No. 133 of 1987 on the question of maintainability and res judicata. 

 13. Mr. Lutfor Rahman Mondal, the learned Advocate for the defendant -respondents, next referred to two misc. cases being Misc. Case No. 233 of 1980 filed by defendant No. 36 and Misc. Case No. 53 of 1981 filed by the heirs of defendant No.38 and defendant No.6 under section 47 CPC objecting the Title Execution Case No. 49 of 1980 filed after passing of the final decree of the partition suit and that in both the Misc. Cases the same point of fraud was raised by the petitioners saying that they were not properly represented and that the final decree was passed against some dead persons and that this Nilufa was shown major being a minor at the time of substitution of the heirs of deceased Sekandar Ali Bepari. The learned Advocate submits that both the Misc. cases were dismissed after full hearing and that the petitioners went upto the Appellate Division against the dismissal judgment passed analogously by the trial Court. The learned Advocate submits that this High Court Division affirmed the judgment holding that the substitution was made on a sworn statement of the heirs of the deceased defendant No. 42 and that this Nilufa or any one of them did not raise any objection against such statement made by themselves but now that point was raised only at the instance of other persons and that this finding of the High Court Division was upheld by the Appellate Division with the observation that this is a complete answer to the contention as put forward on behalf of the petitioners. Mr. Lutfor Rahman Mondal submits that this is a decision of the highest court and this decision has totally closed the question of alleged fraud in the substitution of Nilufa Begum along with all her co-heirs of deceased Sekandar Ali and that this decision of the highest court is binding on this court and Subordinate Court. We find that this is a decision of the Appellate Division of this Court while summarily rejecting the Civil petition for leave No.457 of 1982 filed by the petitioners of the above mentioned two Misc. Cases raising the question of minority of Nilufa Begum also. In the facts and circumstances and the papers as are available in the paper book we find that the question of fraud as raised by plaintiff Nilufa Begum in the matter of the substitution in TS No. 92 of 1966 has already been finally decided upto the highest Court and we think that there is no scope to reagitate that question again in the form of a fresh suit. 

 Mr. Lutfor Rahman Mondal, the learned Advocate for the defendant-respondents, referred to a case of 164 of 1985 filed by one Golapjan Bibi with the similar attempt of setting aside the final decree of partition suit No. 92 of 1966 on the selfsame ground of decree against dead persons and that she was not made party and that this Nilufa Begum being minor was shown to be major while substituting herein the suit. Subsequently, that Golapjan Bibi filed application for withdrawal of the suit and at that time defendant No.57 filed an application for transposition which was allowed by the Subordinate Judge and in revision being Civil Revision No.135 of 1987 this Court also discharged the Rule vide order dated 16-11-1989 against which the present defendant went to the Appellate Division in CA No. 40 of 1990 and the appeal was allowed and the order of the courts below were set aside and the petition for transposition filed by the defendant No.57 was rejected with the similar finding that the matter is closed and passed and the question as raised by defendant No.57 cannot be agitated as the matter was a closed and passed matter and then the suit was dismissed for non prosecution. Mr. Lutfor Rahman Mondal submits that all this is an unprecedented kind of prolognation of a litigation in respect of self same subject matter raised by different persons at different times and in different names coming upto the Appellate Division with the sole aim of undoing a final decree passed by Subordinate Judge in Title Suit No. 92 of 1966 and that the same process of prolongation is still continuing by the present plaintiff Nilufa but that there must be an end of such litigation. 

 19. It may be mentioned here that principle of justice is that there must be an end to litigation but in the volume of facts and circumstances of this case starting from 1966 it appears that different attempts are being made by different persons to defeat a hard earned decree obtained by the original plaintiff Suburnnessa and 2 others in the partition Suit No. 92 of 1966 after a labour of about 25 years making a prolongation of a litigation in respect of same subject matter and same question which should not be allowed to continue. 

 20. Considering all the above facts, circumstances and the papers and documents as are available in 2 paper books and the discussion as we have made above, we find that the learned Subordinate Judge is quite justified in putting an end to a fruitless Title Suit No. 133 of 1987 on the point of law of maintainability and the res judicata. We do not find anything for us to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree passed by the Subordinate Judge, we find no substance in this appeal.
justice_names: Mr. Justice Shah Abu Nayeem Mominur Rahman

parties:
Abul Bashar (Alhaj), being dead his legal heirs (1a) Hosne Ara Begum & ors ------ Petitioners 
VS
Bangladesh represented through the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration, Bangladesh Secretariat, Dhaka and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
6. With the approval of the Cabinet and on obtaining the opinion of the Ministry of Law and Justice, the Ministry of Land Administration gave a general direction to all the Secretaries concerned by Memo No. DA-72/84/514 dated 30-8-84 (Annexure- B) informing that a decision had been taken that if an acquired land was left unused beyond any justifiable time then it should be released in favour of the original owner without referring to the requiring authority or organisation for whose use the land was acquired. 

 7. By a further memo No. DA-72/84/26-acqn dated 9-12-84 issued by the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, the Government of Bangladesh reaffirmed the earlier policy for surrendering the unused lands for their utilisation for productive purpose (Annexure-C). Based on the policy of the Government, the said Ministry vide a Memo dated 22-5-86 asked the Deputy Commissioner concerned to send considered opinion whether to release the requisitioned case land in favour of the original owners (Annexure-D). 

 8. On 13-9-89 the petitioners made a representation to the respondent No. 2 the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong in which they mentioned that though the land was requisitioned for creating residential plots but the same had not been used for the said purpose. The petitioners further requested the respondent No. 2 to release the unutilised land to the original owners (Annexure-E). 

 9. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) Chittagong vide his memo No. 739/LA dated 27-5-90 addressed to the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reform informed that all lands acquired by the Chittagong Development Authority could not be used for the purpose for which they were acquired, one of which is the disputed case land. The Additional Deputy Commissioner recommended that the case land may be released in favour of the original owners who are poor and still residing there. 

 14. It is further stated in the affidavit-in- opposition that the compensation for the lands thus requisitioned was assessed under LA Case No. 138/62-63 based on the prevailing market price of the land in the vicinity then. Therefore, adequate compensation was made over to the original owners as per relevant provisions of Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948. It is further stated that no homestead and graveyard were acquired and the land in question is being used based on the Annual Development Programme. 

 18. Mr. M Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, has argued that the requisition and acquisition process of the case land had started in the year 1964, more than twenty eight years back, but so far only part compensation has been paid and the full payment has remained unpaid. Moreover, the compensation is so low that it cannot be considered adequate. But from the record it appears 90% of the compensation money assessed has already been handed over to the original owners and only 10% is yet to be paid. It also appears that the compensation is assessed under LA Case No. 138/62-63 on the basis of the prevailing market price then There is no evidence on record to show that any objection was raised by the petitioners while accepting the 90% of the compensation. Now, after twenty-eight years we do not find any reason for this court in its writ jurisdiction to enter into the disputed question of adequacy or inadequacy of the compensation assessed. 

 19. By referring to Article 42(1) and (2) of the Constitution Mr. Islam next challenged the very vires of (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 on the ground that no clear guideline for payment of compensation has been provided in it. Article 42 guarantees that no person shall be deprived of his property by way of acquisition, nationalisation and requisition save by authority of law that provides for compensation and specifies the principle on which, and the manner in which the compensation is to be assessed and paid. We however do not find any substance in the contention of the learned Advocate that the Act does not provide guideline for payment of compensation. Section 5(B) of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 provides that when a property is requisitioned under section 5(3) with a view to its permanent acquisition, the owner of the property shall be offered or paid in advance before possession is taken over, compensation to the extent of either 100% for structure and building and 90% for lands of the provisional estimate. From annexure F to the writ petition we find that the owners of the case land had already accepted 90% of advance compensation. Moreover, section 7 of the said Act lays down the manner and principle for payment of compensation for immovable property. Sub-section (aaa) of section 7 further provides for arbitration in case of non-acceptance of compensation by the land owners and sub-sections c, cc, d and e of section 7 lay down how an arbitrator shall proceed in calculating the market value of the land requisitioned. From the record it does not appear that the original owners went for arbitration complaining the adequacy of the compensation. 

 25. A reading of Annexure-C, specially its last paragraph, shows the Government's concern about the unutilised lands that are lying with the requiring authorities, after completion of projects, for which they were requisitioned. It urges the requiring bodies to return those lands to the owners if they are not used within a reasonable time. Otherwise, it states that such lands would be released by the Government in favour of the original owners without referring the matter to the requiring authority or Ministry for whose use the lands have been requisitioned or acquired. A long time has lapsed since the issuance of the letter but the Government has not taken any step in that direction. On the other hand it appears that the Ministry that issued the letter for return of unused lands had itself refused to release the case land by Annexure G. It may be noted here that the Ministry that issued the said letter and the Ministry that refused to release the case land are the same. The Ministry of Land and the Chittagong Development Authority are very much the relevant authorities to decide what land they may return for being excess and unutilised land It has been held in the case of Badal Rani Misra vs. Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR (AD) 68 (relevant para-12). 

 27. The learned Advocate for the petitioners then raises the point that the case land has not yet been vested in the Government The original owners are still the legal owners of the case land. Non vesting of the land even after 28 years of requisition shows that the case land is not required for the purpose for which it was acquired. Therefore, the case land should be derequisitioned and returned to the original owners. Here by referring to Sat yam Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. vs. Calcutta Improvement Trust AIR 1989 263 Mr. Amirul Islam argues that the petitioners are well within their right to challenge the requisition for long and inordinate delay by the acquisition authority in concluding the acquisition proceeding. We have gone through the decision and, in our view, the decision referred to is not applicable in the instant case as the facts and circumstances are different. In that case certain land was purchased by a Housing Society and after getting clearance from Calcutta Improvement Trust it started construction of five apartment buildings for its members. While the construction was in progress and a substantial part was completed the Society was asked to stop work and was informed that the acquisition proceeding in respect of the land was pending for a long time. Under the circumstances the Court held that inordinate delay on the part of the acquisition authority can be a cause of action. This is not the case here. Petitioners came to know about the requisition immediately on requisition of the property but neither objected nor went for arbitration rather accepted a substantial part of the compensation. 

 29. From the facts of the case Mr. Amirul Islam argues that except 5.79 acres of land, rest of the lands requisitioned have already been acquired, but the case land has not been acquired as it is not within the proposed development project. It is a chunk of land separate from the rest. From the record it appears that the case land was handed over to the Steel and Engineering Corporation by the requiring body for a housing project of the said Corporation. But subsequently, it was taken back when the Corporation failed to start the project. The respondents claim this as the reason for the delay in starting their own project. The respondents also submit that under the Emergency Requisition Act 1948 there is no bar to use any requisitioned property for a purpose other than the purpose for which it is requisitioned. We find substance in this argument. We have already taken the view that the acquisition process is not yet concluded and continuing and therefore we are not inclined to hold that the case land was not included in the original project. 

 31. Mr. Kamal-ul-Alam, the learned Advocate for the Respondent No. 4 (CDA), has submitted that this application is not maintainable inasmuch as the petitioners are not aggrieved persons and because it involves disputed questions of facts as to whether the petitioners are successors-in-interest of the original owners from whom the land had been requisitioned and whether they are in possession or not. It appears from the record that the order of requisition has never been denied nor it was challenged either under sub-section 1 or 2 of section 5 of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948. On the other hand, this petition was filed originally by 59 petitioners though some others were substituted later. Out of 59 petitioners only petitioner Nos. 1 and 2 have given their father's name. Other petitioners have simply stated at the end of the list of their names that all the petitioners are from Faridapara PS Chandgaon, District Chittagong. The writ petition does not mention the name of the fathers of the petitioner Nos. 3-59. The petitioners also do not specifically state to which particular area of the 5.79, acres of the case land each petitioner is laying claim. Not even the title deeds of the original owners are annexed to the writ petition in support of the petitioners' claim for ownership. Whether the petitioners are the genuine heirs of the original owners remains a disputed question of fact and cannot be decided without evidence. 

 33.  The petitioners claim also suffers from laches and delay. The case land was requisitioned in the year 1964 and the writ petition was filed in 1992, almost after 28 years. It seems to us that the writ petition under Article 102 has been filed after an inordinate delay during which lot of changes have taken place regarding the disputed land. Under the circumstances this Division Bench is loath to exercise its writ jurisdiction. The statement made by the petitioners that during this time they have been trying elsewhere for the derequisition of case land is vague and without material. Save the recommendation of the Deputy Commissioner in 1990 based on an application dated 13-9-89, (Annexure-E), by the petitioner No. 1 no other material has been given. From this it appears that it is only around later part of 1980 the petitioner No. 1 woke up to file an application for himself and others for derequisition of the case land. Extraordinary remedy provided by writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution is a speedy relief meant for the vigilant not for indolent. It is by now well settled that laches and delay disentitles one to seek remedy before writ jurisdiction.

parties:
Akhtar Banu being dead her heirs: Alhaj Md. Hossain Khan and others ------ Plaintiff-Appellants
VS.
Habibunessa and others ------ Defendant-Respondents
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ : This appeal by the plaintiffs following leave is from judgment and order dated 6 March 1986 passed by a Single Judge of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 420 of 1985 making the Rule absolute and holding the Title Suit No. 245 of 1985 of the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge. Dhaka abated as a whole for non-substitution of the heirs of deceased-defendant No. 3. Aga Ali Hasan Raza, within time who had died on 4-4-1972. 

 3. To recall briefly the facts of the case the predecessor of the appellants. Akhtar Banu, instituted Title Suit No. 9 of 1957 in the aforesaid Court for declaration of title to and for recovery and confirmation of possession in certain parts of the suit land. The suit on transfer to the 5th Court of the Subordinate Judge. Dhaka was renumbered as Title Suit No. 107 of 1959 and again on further transfer to the original Court was renumbered as Title Suit No. 245 of 1985. On 12-8-1969 the plaintiff came to know that defendant No. 4 had died and accordingly filed Miscellaneous Case No. 25 of 1969 on 28-8-69 for substitution of his heirs after setting aside abatement. The learned Subordinate Judge however suomotu recorded the abatement of the suit as a whole by his order dated 10-9-69 on account of the death of defendant No. 4. On 15-4-72 a lawyer of opposite party No. 3 (defendant No. 3) in the aforesaid misc. case informed the Court that the said opposite party had died on 4-4-72 whereupon the petitioner (plaintiff) prayed for time for substituting the heirs of the deceased opposite party No. 3. On 13-5-72 the learned Subordinate Judge passed the following order on the substitution petition filed by the plaintiff petitioner: "The OP files hajira, petitioner prays for substitution in place of deceased OP No. 3, on the grounds as stated therein. Heard, prayer is allowed. Let the heirs of the deceased OP 3 (be) substituted. Amend the plaint and the register accordingly. 

 8. It is not disputed that the heirs of deceased-defendant No. 3 Aga Ali Reza were substituted in Mise, Case No. 25 of 1969, the wife of the deceased, Feezza Khanum, having already been on record as defendant No. 2. The learned Judge of the High Court Division took the view that the misc. case was a separate and independent proceeding and substitution made in that misc. case did not automatically substitute the heirs of deceased- defendant No.3 in the suit and that the plaintiffs ought to have taken steps for substitution of the heirs of the deceased-defendant after the abatement matter (on the death of defendant No. 4) was finally disposed of by this Division and the records came back to the original Court. The learned Judge has gone wrong in taking the aforesaid view and thus allowed himself to a wrong decision. 

 10. In the Privy Council case what happened was that in the course of the hearing of a suit in the Court of the District Judge, Ferozpur an application was made to the Chief Court of Punjab to revise an order of the District Judge directing the production of certain books. During the pendency of the matter in the Chief Court several of the parties died and substitutions were made in the proceeding in the Chief Court on ex parte applications. Then after the record when back from the Chief Court to the District Judge an application was made by one of the defendants for an order of abatement of the suit on the ground that the heirs of the deceased parties hat not been brought on the record of the suit within time. One District Judge ordered the abatement of the suit. A successor District Judge, however, set aside the order of abatement. The Chief Court set aside the latter order on the ground that a successor District Judge could not review an order of his predecessor. The Privy Council, however, allowed the appeal and remitted the case of the original Court to proceed with the hearing of the case on merit holding that in the circumstances no question of abatement arose. It is in this context that the Privy Council laid down the rule as aforesaid which is being followed consistently in the courts of the subcontinent including those of ours.

2. Opposite party Nos.1-2 as plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 301 of 1979 in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Kushtia against the petitioner and other opposite parties for declaration of their title in the suit land and the said suit was being contested by the petitioner by filing written statement On 4.4.77 trial Court directed the plaintiff-opposite parties to take steps for service of fresh summons upon defendant No. 2. But the plaintiffs having failed to take any step on 30.4.77 the plaintiffs were directed to show cause why the suit shall not be dismissed and fixed 21.5.77 for the purpose. But the plaintiffs having not taken any step nor shown cause the suit was dismissed for default on 21.5.77. Thereafter plaintiffs filed Miscellaneous Case No. 98 of 1979 under Order 9 rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 18.9.79 for setting aside the said order of dismissal of the suit mainly on the allegation that their tadbirker Tofazzel Hossain who looked after the suit was gained over by the defendants and in collusion with them he allowed the suit to be dismissed for default which fact the plaintiffs came to know only on 15.9.79 after enquiry from the Court through the Advocate's clerk. That case was contested by the petitioner by filing a written objection and also by adducing evidence. But after the close of the evidence plaintiffs amended the case title of the said miscellaneous case as one under Order 9 rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure as none of the parties was present on the date of dismissal of the suit. By the judgment and order dated 14.9.81 trial Court dismissed the miscellaneous case. On appeal by the plaintiffs by the impugned judgment Court of appeal below allowed the appeal and restored the suit. 

 7. It has already been found that the Court of appeal below had no jurisdiction to entertain Miscellaneous Appeal No. 94 of 1981 and to pass the impugned judgment allowing the appeal. So the impugned judgment in honest in the eye of law. But as I have already found that the judgment dated 14.9.81 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in Misc. Case No. 98 of 1979 suffers from error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice, I set aside the said order and restore Title Suit No. 301 of 1979 to its original file and number. 

 8. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment dated 25.2.85 passed by the Additional District Judge, Kushtia in Misc. Appeal No. 94 of 1981 as well as judgment and order dated 14.9.81 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Kushtia in Misc. Case No. 98 of 1979 are set aside and Title Suit No. 301 of 1979 is restored to its original file and number.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No. 421 of 1968.
parties:
Nehal Uddin (Md) and others ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Amena Khatunand others ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This second appeal by the defendant-appellants is directed against the judgment and decree dated 30.12.67 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Rangpur in Title Appeal No. 54 of 1966 reversing those dated 9.2.66 passed by the learned Munsif, 1st Court, Rangpur. 

 2. Plaintiffs case, in short, is that the land hereinafter called the suit-property covered by Khatian No. 14 (Ext. 2) of Mouza Marichbari within PS Mithapukur originally belonged to one Farahtullah to the extent of eight annas, to one Shariatullah to the extent of four annas and to one Kamiran and Samiran each, to the extent of two annas. Then Farahtullah died leaving behind defendant No. 1 as his wife, father of defendant Nos. 2-4 as his sons, defendants Nos. 5 and 6 namely Tasiran and Farijan as his daughters. The defendant I as per kabala Ext. I sold her share along with that of her daughters defendant Nos. 5 and 6 (then minors) to the plaintiff as far back as in 1348 BS. The same kabala was executed also by defendant No. 7, son of Samiran purporting to transfer the whole of his share. Two years later, father of defendant Nos. 2-4 also sold 0.55 acres of land to the plaintiff vide kabala Ext. I(a). Thereafter in 1352 BS.Farijan Nesa sold her 0.45 acres of land as per kabala Ext. 1(b).
