Afterwards the plaintiff Amena Khatun herself sold to the defendant Nos. 12-15 1.34 acres of land in 1363 B.S. and 1364 B.S. vide Kabala Exts I(c)-I(d) out of her kabala purchased lands covered by Exts. 1-1(b). Since her purchase of the lands, the plaintiff has been in ejmali possession of the suit-land with the other co-sharers in the suit property. The lands sold to the defendant Nos. 12-15 are being possessed by themselves. But as the ejmali possession of the suit-land has been fraught with inconvenience and as the share of the defendant Nos. 5 and 6 has been wrongly and collusively recorded in their names the plaintiff has been constrained to institute the present suit for declaration of her title to 1.26 acres of land and for partition of her total of 2.48 acres of land. 

 2. Has the Plaintiff acquired any title to and has she been in possession of any portion of the suit property, if so, to what extent? 

 3. To what relief (s), if any, is the plaintiff entitled. 

 6. The learned Munsif on consideration of the evidence on record decided issue No. I in favour of the contesting defendants and against the plaintiff. As regards issue No. 2 the Trial Court held that the plaintiff as per Ext’s. 1-lb was not entitled to get more than a total of 2.24 acres of land. But consequently upon her sale of 1.34 acres, vide Ext’s. 1(c) to 1(d) to defendant Nos. 12-15 she was not supposed to get more than 0.90 acres of land. As regards possession of the plaintiff in the suit land, the trial Court found relying only on the deposition of DW 4 that the plaintiff was in possession of some portion of the suit jota and as such was entitled to get partition with respect to only 0.90 acres of land appertaining to the jota. With the above findings, the trial Court partly decreed the suit on contest in the preliminary form against defendants No. 2-6, ex pane against the rest by his judgment and decree dated 9.2.66. 

 7. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and declared plaintiffs title to the extent of 1.26 acres of land and allowed partition of the total 2.48 acres of land in her favour in the suit jote by his judgment and decree dated 30.12.67. 

 9. Mr. Md. Shahjahan, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellants, has taken me through the judgments of both the Courts below and then submitted that so far the transfer of the shares of the properties of the defendant Nos. 5 and 6 in the suit jote by their mother during their minority in favour of the plaintiff-respondent by a registered deed vide Ext. 1 was void ab initio and both the Courts concurrently came to the aforesaid finding on the basis of the decision of the famous leading case of Immambandi and others Vs. Mutsaddi and others reported in 45 IA 73. Hence, that finding is final and conclusive and cannot be disturbed in this second appeal. His next submission is that the lower appellate Court committed error of law in holding that the interest of the defendant Nos. 5-6 to the extent of 1.26 acres of land was extinguished under section 28 of the Limitation Act and the plaintiff-respondent acquired title of the said land belonging to the defendant Nos. 5-6 by way of adverse possession, and as such the impugned judgment and decree of the lower Appellate Court cannot be sustained in law. In this connection he submits that the question of adverse possession was neither pleaded in the plaint nor any such claim has been proved by reliable evidence, but the lower appellate Court without due consideration of this aspect of the case and the evidence on record most illegally and arbitrarily observed as follows: 

 "Naturally it is now with defendants 2 to 4 to put claim to the interest of defendant Nos. 5 and 6. But in view, of my above discussion regarding possession, it is my considered view that the plaintiff was in possession of Ext. 1 land since her purchase in 1941 for more than 12 years and as the defendants 5 and 6 did not sue the purchaser (plaintiff) within 12 years from the date of sale or within 3 years from the date of their attaining majority, whichever is later, to restore and protect their title, their claim is barred under section 28 of the Limitation Act". 

 and upon such observation illegally declared the tight, title, and interest of the plaintiff over 1.26acres of land of defendant Nos. 5 and 6 in the suit property. Mr. Shahjahan further submits referring to the plaint as well as to the evidence on record that it is the case of the plaintiff-respondent that she is in ejmali possession of the suit property and further by way of purchase by registered deed Ext. 1 not only from minor defendant Nos. 5 and 6 but also from defendant Nos. 1 and 7 the plaintiff became a co-sharer in the suit jote. But a co-sharer cannot claim title by way of adverse possession against another co-sharer unless ouster of the later co-sharer from the land in question is established by evidence. In the instant case there being no finding on discussion of evidence on record as to any such ouster of the contesting defendants 5 and 6 from the disputed suit-property, the claim of title by adverse possession by the plaintiff cannot be legally sustained and the interest of the said defendants can not be held to have been extinguished or barred under section 28 of the Limitation Act. In support of his contention, Mr. Shahajahan has referred to a decision in the case of Sonaullah Hawlader Vs. Apseruddin Bali and others reported in 7 DLR 514 wherein it has been held that by a Division Bench that- 

 "possession of a co-sharer to be considered from three aspects; (1) Among co-sharers themselves possession of one co-owner is possession of all, to claim adverse possession in such a case assertion must be notoriously and unequivocally hostile. (2) A stranger purchaser of an undivided share getting possession of some specific land stands on the same footing as the other co-sharers, the land purchased by him being the land to be allotted to the share of his vendor on partition. (3) A stranger purchaser from a co-sharer who sold the property and the purchaser possessing it openly as of right without any attempt at concealment so that any person interested may know about his exclusive possession on the basis of his purchase, in such a case the purchaser's possession is not that of a co-sharer but it is exclusive possession in assertion of his title on the basis of his purchase." 

 12. Mr. Akrm Hossain Amin, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, submits that even if the claim of title by way of adverse possession is not pleaded in the plaint still it will not be a bar in allowing the claim of plaintiff's title by way of adverse possession if he is found in continuous possession of the suit land in assertion of his title for more than 12 years, hence, in the instant case, possession of the plaintiff in the suit land for more than 12 years extinguished the right, title and interest of the original owners i.e. defendants 5 and 6 under section 28 of the Limitation Act. In support of his contention, he has cited a decision in the case of Sadak Ali Vs. Surju Ali & others reported in 7 DLR 94, wherein it has been held that: 

 "Possession under a mistake or invalid title is as effective as that of a trespasser, and, if sufficient in the length of time and continuity, gives the holder a good title.... 

 The mere fact that the plaintiff did not specifically claim title by adverse possession is no reason to disentitle him to the decree which he is otherwise, entitled". 

 "If the owner whose property is encroached upon suffers his right to be barred by the law of Limitation the practical effect is the extension of his title in favour of the party in possession. Consequently where the executor holds the property adversely to the heir for upwards of 12 years on behalf of the charity for which it was dedicated, the title to it acquired by prescription, becomes vested in the charity and that of the heir if he had any, becomes extinguished by operation of s. 28" 

 14. Relying on this Mr. Khan contends that the plaintiff has acquired title to the share of defendant Nos. 5 and 6 in the suit property to the extent of 1.26 acres of land by way of adverse possession, if not by their purchase by registered deed Ext. 1 and therefore, the lower appellate Court has rightly declared plaintiffs title to the disputed 1.26 acres of land and allowed partition of the total share of the plaintiff to the extent of 2.48 acres of land. 

 15. Before considering the above submission of the learned Advocates of both the sides, let me keep on record some admitted facts in this case. Firstly, defendant No 1 for herself and as mother guardian of defendants Nos 5 and 6 executed and registered the deed of sale vide Ext I in favour of the plaintiff Amena Khatun predecessor of the present respondents including the shares of defendants 5 and 6 to the extent of 1.26 acres of land during their minority. Secondly the plaintiff respondent purchased in all 3,82 acres of land vide Ext. 1, 1 (a),- 1 (b) and out of this 3,82 acres, she had sold out 1.34 acres of land. So, the plaintiffs present claim was confined to the extent of 2.48 acres of land only. The dispute is mainly with regard to 1.26 acres of land of the shares of defendant Nos 5 and 6. If the plaintiff could establish her right, title and interest over the disputed 1.26 acres of land, then she would get her entire 2.48 acres of land in the suit holding and if she could not, in that case she would be entitled to get only 1.22 acres of land. Now, let me see whether the plaintiff has been able to establish her title over the disputed land of 1.26 acres. It may be pointed out that the claim of title over this disputed property by virtue of the registered sale deed Ext. 1 executed on behalf of the minor defendants 5 and 6 has been lost, being void ab initio as has been concurrently found by both the courts below. Now, it is to be seen whether the plaintiff respondent has been able to establish title by way of adverse possession over the said property i.e. 1.26 acres of land. The decisions cited at the Bar are not disputed but main question is whether the plaintiffs claim for any exclusive and actual possession over the specific portion of the disputed land of the defendants 5 and 6 has been proved by sufficient reliable evidence to be open, notorious and in assertion of her title for more than 12 years. This question ought to have been properly discussed and decided on consideration of the evidence on record, but unfortunately the trial Court without doing so only observed as follows: 

 22. Now, from the consideration and analysis of the above evidence, it appears that the plaintiff claimed possession over the disputed portion of the suit jote in three different ways, firstly, for 10/11 years through some bargadars and again through khas possession for 4/5 years and then again through the present defendants 2-4 but these defendants stated that they were bargadars under defendant Nos. 5 and 6 and used to give crops to the said defendant Nos. 5 and 6 and after their own purchase, they have been possessing suit property independently as their own. It is the case of the plaintiff that she was in ejmali possession of the suit property and admittedly there has been no partition of the suit property by metes and bounds. Furthermore, from the deposition of the DW 4, it appear that the suit property was recorded in the present khatians in the names of the Air Tran defendants including the names of defendant Nos. 5 and 6. It is of course true that the record of right cannot be a document of title but it may be used as documentary evidence to show possession. Now, title by way of adverse possession has been claimed by the plaintiff and as such the onus is upon the plaintiff to establish the conditions required for acquisition of title by adverse possession. In view of the decisions cited above, it is no doubt clear that in the case of a claim of title by adverse possession by a co-sharer against another co-sharer, ouster of the latter has to be proved and possession of the party claiming title by adverse possession must be actual and exclusive for a continuous period of more than 12 years in assertion of hostile title. From the evidence on record as discussed above, it does not appear that the plaintiff has been able to fulfill the above conditions by reliable and sufficient evidence. It is rather the case of the plaintiff that she possessed the suit property in ejmali with other co-sharers through bargadars, but she could not lead any evidence to prove ouster of the other co-sharers particularly defendant Nos. 5 and 6 from their portion of the suit lands. 

 23. In that view of the matter, I must hold that the interest of the defendant Nos. 5 and 6 in respect of 1.26 acres of land in the suit jote has not been extinguished or barred under section 28 of the Limitation Act and the plaintiff respondent has not acquired any right, title or interest over the said disputed portion of the suit land i.e., 1.26 acres of the suit land by way of adverse possession claimed. Hence the lower appellate Court has committed error of law in allowing the claim of acquisition of plaintiff's title to the extent of 1.26 acres of land in respect of the shares of the defendant Nos. 5-6 in the suit jota and directing partition of the same by metes and bounds along with other lands measuring 1.22 acres i.e. partition for 2.48 acres in total. 

 24. For the reasons stated above the impugned judgment and decree of the court of appeal below are liable to be set aside. The plaintiff is entitled to get a decree only for his 1.22 acres of land in the suit property and not for the remaining 1.26 acres. The suit is accordingly decreed in part and the plaintiff can get partition of his 1.22 acres of land only by metes and bounds.

parties:
Mohiuddin Ahmed and others  ------- Petitioners.
Vs.
Lutfur Rahman and another  ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
This is an application under section 38 of the Companies Act, 1913 for rectification of the share register of the company respondent No.2 in respect of the shares of the petitioners originally held by them in the aforesaid company and for inserting their names in the share register of the company in place of respondent No.1. 

 3. In addition to the aforesaid agreement dated 8.3.85 another agreement was executed by the petitioner No. 1 and respondent No. 1 on 15.7.85, as the respondent No. 1 was unable to fulfil the terms and conditions as per agreement dated 8.3.85. Under the 2nd agreement a deadline of 31.3.1986 was fixed within which period the respondent No. 1 must get the house properties at 109, Hrishikesh Das Road, Dhaka together with the press and machineries released from the charge of Pubali Bank. Full and final payment of Taka ten lacs would be made within 30.7.86 as it was fixed in previous agreement. It is further stated that the petitioners fulfilled all terms of the aforesaid agreement. They withdrew the money suits filed against the respondent No. 1 and duly transferred their shares in favour of the respondent No.1 . In the above agreement dated 15.7.85 it was stipulated that in case the respondent No. 1 does not fulfil the terms of the agreement or is unable to clear the Pubali Bank charges and get the mortgaged properties as stated above released in favour of the petitioner No. 1 by 31.3.76, then this agreement along with the agreement dated 8.3.85 shall be treated as cancelled and the petitioners would get back their respective shares in the said company and they would be restored to their original position in the company and the respondent No. 1 would be liable for compensation as claimed by the petitioner No. 1. In the said agreement respondent No. 1 also took the responsibility to take over all the liabilities of the company which were with the Ministry of Industries, Collector of Customs, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, Bangladesh Shilpa Bank, Investment Corporation of Bangladesh, Pubali Bank Ltd., Bank of Credit and Commerce International and also other liabilities of the respondent No. 2 company and get the petitioner No. 1 relieved of all his obligations from the aforesaid creditors by giving written clearance. The first agreement dated 8.3.85 is annexed as Annexure "A" and the second agreement dated 15.7.85 is annexed as Annexure "B" to the application. 

 7. It is further stated that this application under section 38 of the Companies Act is not maintainable inasmuch as in the agreement the respondent No. 2 company was not a party. As the shares had already been transferred and registered in favour of the respondent No. 1, the petitioners relief does not lie under the Companies Act. It is further alleged that in the present case there are so many disputed questions of facts which cannot be adjudicated in such summary proceeding. It is their further case that the petitioners committed forgery in the subsequent agreement by inserting the last sentence in the last paragraph of the said agreement, although the said sentence was not there originally. Such alteration is very material, which affects the very intent and spirit, and has totally changed the character of the agreement. In the affidavit in-opposition the respondent Nos. l and 2 have annexed the photo copies of the instruments of transfer and the shares certificates vide Annexure 1-96. 

 In this letter it is certified that M/s Paper Converting and Packaging Ltd. Karim Chamber, 99 Motijheel CA, Dhaka, Bangladesh, has repaid the settled amount in full as per agreement and at present has got no liability with the bank. It was filed by a supplementary affidavit. After the aforesaid certificate dated 2.4.90 the respondent No.1 had written two letters to the Managing Director, Pubali Bank, one dated 4.4.90 and another dated 11.4.90 for releasing the properties and handing over the title deeds of the land and house properties remaining with the Pubali Bank. The petitioners also filed a reply to the aforesaid supplementary affidavit filed by the respondent No. 1. 

 16. It is also stipulated in the agreement that the petitioner shall transfer and hand over all their movable and immovable properties which they were entitled to the Paper Converting and Packing Ltd., Karim Chamber (Ground Floor), 99, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dhaka, M/s Monospool Paper Products Ltd. Corn Flour Mills Ltd. and the properties situated at Kamarkhali pruchased by the Company in the name of Rabindra Nath Bose. In this agreement petitioner No. 1 and respondent No. 1 put their signatures and the wife and sons of the petitioner no. 1 also put their signatures as witness in the document. 

 19. In the second part of Paragraph 1 of the agreement dated 15.7.85 it is stipulated that if for any reason the respondent No.1 does not fulfill the undertaking he had taken or as per his undertaking if he does not hand over the mortgaged properties after releasing it from the said Pubali Bank within the specified time, or if he fails to fulfill his commitment, then the subsequent agreement dated 15.7.85 along with the agreement dated 8.3.85 would be considered as cancelled and according to the claim of the petitioner No. 1, respondent No. 1 will be liable for all compensation for damages. It is also stipulated in the last sentence of the agreement that in such a situation the petitioners will naturally be considered to be restored to their original right and title in the company. As regards this last sentence the respondent No.1 had taken objection to the effect that this is a subsequent alteration and addition and this is a forgery for which the entire agreement is void. I will consider this objection separately with regard to this last sentence later on. 

 20. Let me see first whether the petitioners have been able to fulfill the terms and conditions of the agreements, or the respondent No. 1 had failed to perform his part of the agreements. The petitioners have categorically stated in their application that in pursuance of the aforesaid two agreements, though in the eye of law one agreement, the petitioners have fulfilled all the terms and conditions and they transferred all their shares in the company in favour of the respondent No. 1 and they had withdrawn the two money suits against the respondents. There was no monetary consideration for transferring these shares to respondent No. 1, rather only consideration was the terms and conditions of the agreement on which the petitioners transferred their shares to the respondent No. 1. In the affidavit-in-opposition, this statement of the petitioners has not been at all denied. Their assertion that they have waived all their rights and title in other properties as mentioned in the agreement has also not been denied by the respondents. So, from the application and affidavit-in-opposition and other papers filed by both the parties, it appears that the petitioners have fulfilled all the terms of the agreements as they were required to do. 

 23. In the background of all the documents and papers submitted before the Court, Mr. M Nurullah, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that there was no violation of the terms of the aforesaid agreements by the petitioners and there was no allegation to that effect also. He further submits that the time is the essence of the contract and since the documents and papers produced before the Court have unmistakably shown that the respondent No.1 had failed to pay Tk. 10 lacs to the petitioner No.1 and also failed to get the mortgaged properties of the petitioner No.1 released from Pubali Bank within the stipulated time according to the terms of the agreements, the agreements stood cancelled by operation of the terms of the agreement and the petitioners reverted back to their original position as on 8.3.85. 

 24. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondents, on the other hand, submits that as regards payment of Tk.10 lacs, since the petitioner No.1 refused to take the money the respondent No.1 was unable to pay it. This submission of Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed has not been substantiated by any paper on record. Rather the paper namely, the letter of Mr. RN Chakraborty, the Chief Accountant, dated 14.10.86 clearly shows that Tk.25,000.00 was offered after the last date of payment of installment as the last date was 30.7.86. Petitioner No. 1. and respondent No.1 are full brothers. Money was to be paid by the respondent No.1 to the Petitioner No.1 as per terms of the agreement. It is difficult to understand why Mr. RN Chakraborty was dragged in this matter of payment of money to the petitioner No.1. Respondent No.1 could have issued a cheque or bank draft in favour of the petitioner No.1 and sent it by registered post. If it was refused, then such a contention could be given some weight. Further, it could not be shown that by the last date i.e. 30.7.86 the respondent No.1 offered the remaining amount of Tk. 10 lacs to the petitioner No.1, because the alleged offer of Tk. 25,000.00 does not fulfill the terms of the agreement. Since the respondent No.1 failed to fulfill his own obligation as per terms of the agreement, he is not entitled to get any benefit out of it. 

 27. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed submits that the present application under section 38 of the Companies Act is not maintainable inasmuch as in the agreement the company was not a party and the petitioner Nos. 2-5 were not the signatories of the agreements and as such the petitioners are incompetent to invoke the jurisdiction of this Court under section 38 of the Companies Act. It is not disputed that the petitioner No.1 and respondent No.1 are two brothers. Petitioner No.1 was the Chairman of the Board of Directors and the respondent No.1 was the Managing Director. It is also not disputed that properties of the petitioner No.1 were mortgaged to the Pubali Bank for the aforesaid company respondent No. 2. Since misunderstanding cropped up between the two brothers, one brother and his sons and wife transferred their shares to the respondent No.1 on the terms and conditions as laid down in the two agreements. Petitioners were the real share-holders like the respondent No.1 in the company. This was some sort of package deal in between the members of the same family. Petitioner No.1 and respondent No.1 signed the agreements as parties and the sons and wife of the petitioner No.1 were the witnesses. In pursuance of the terms and conditions of the agreement petitioners sold their all shares to the respondent No.1 without any other monetary consideration excepting the terms and conditions laid down in the agreement. Since it was held above that the agreement stood cancelled for non-fulfillment of the terms and conditions of the agreements by the respondent No.1, petitioners are entitled to revert back to their original position and to have their shares back in the company as they had on 8.3.85. Originally the petitioners were the registered share-holders and now they are praying before this Court for restoring themselves to original position in the company. Section 38 of the Companies Act runs as follows: 

 29. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed further submits that since there are disputed questions of facts involving in the present case which cannot be resolved on filing affidavits, the petitioners are not entitled to invoke the jurisdiction of this Court under section 38 of the Act inasmuch as it is merely a summary proceeding. In every case the facts will be disputed as one party will allege and the other party will deny. But from the materials available on record and on the basis of the facts which in fact cannot be disputed, this Court can decide the matter under section 38 of the Act. No doubt it is a summary proceeding under section 38 of the Act but it is a discretion of the Court to see whether the point at issue can be disposed of and resolved on the basis of the materials available on record. If the case is complicated and very doubtful and if it appears that without resorting to some other procedure a case cannot be disposed of, this Court should not interfere with such a matter. But if it is apparent on the face of the records that legal rights of the parties are clear and the same can be settled on the basis of the materials on record, then this Court can interfere with the matter under section 38 of the Act In the present case it appears to me that the documents and papers filed by the parties are so clear that the rights of the parties can be settled on the basis of those papers and the case can be disposed of accordingly. 

 "The Chief Baron read the later part of section 35. I cannot imagine any language better adopted for conferring a jurisdiction to decide disputes between two alleged members of a company in respect of the title to shares therein. I think, therefore, that the jurisdiction exists." 

 "But the Joint Stock Companies Act 1857 section 9, greatly increased the effect of the earlier enactment, for it expressly gave power to decide questions of title arising between two or more alleged holders of shares. 

 "Looking at all the words of section 35 and giving them a reasonable construction, I think that the legislature intended to give the Court jurisdiction to make an order so as to decide questions of title, trusting to the discretion of the Court not to decide in this summary manner any intricate or difficult question of title; but that, if the Court thinks fit, they have jurisdiction to make the order in all cases." 

 35. Let me now consider the objection raised by Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed as regards the last portion of paragraph 1 of the agreement dated 15.7.85. According to Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, the meaning and interpretation is that if the respondent No. 1 fails to fulfill the terms and conditions of the agreements, the petitioner No.1 will be at liberty to go to the Court and pray for compensation for the alleged damages. Neither the petitioners can come under section 38 of the Companies Act before this Court nor even they are entitled to file a suit for specific performance of contract under the Specific Relief Act. It is difficult to accept the contention of Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, because this is not the correct interpretation of the concluding portion of paragraph 1 of the agreement dated 15.7.85. It has clearly prescribed that if within the stipulated time the respondent No. 1 fails to fulfill the terms and conditions of the agreement, the agreement dated 15.7.85 along with agreement dated 8.3.85 shall stand cancelled and I have already held that for non-fulfillment of the terms and conditions by the respondent No.1 these two agreements stood cancelled and the petitioners reverted back to their original position as share-holders of the company. Not only that, the petitioners would get their rights and interests back as they had previously in the said company and in other properties as covered by those agreements. 

 39. In this connection it may be mentioned that in paragraph 11 of the affidavit-in-opposition the respondent No.1 has tried to make out a story of inserting the last sentence in the agreement dated 15.7.85 at a subsequent date. It is alleged that the petitioner No.1 got both the original and duplicate copies of the agreement dated 15.7.85 signed by the respondent No.1, but with malafide intention the petitioner No.1 did not hand over the duplicate copy of the agreement to the respondent No.1. Such allegations have been totally denied by the petitioners in paragraph 9 of their affidavit-in-reply slating that such allegations are totally false, concocted and motivated. It is difficult to believe this story as the respondent No.1 has tried to make out in paragraph 11 of the affidavit-in-opposition. Both the petitioner No.1 and the respondent No.1 had put their signatures and their eldest brother Shahabuddin Ahmed put his signature as witness in the agreement dated 15.7.85. Petitioner No.1 has stated that the duplicate copy of the agreement was given to the respondent No.1. After the agreement was executed the respondent NO.1 had done so many things and made so many correspondences in this matter. 

 "If an alteration (by erasure interlineations or otherwise) is made in a material part of a deed after its execution, by or with the consent of any party thereto or person entitled thereunder, but without the consent of the party of parties liable thereunder, the deed is thereby made void. The avoidance however is not ab initio or so as to nullify any conveyancing effect which the deed has already had; but only operates as from the time of such alteration and so as to prevent the person who has made or authorised the alteration and those claiming under him, from putting the deed in suit to enforce, against any party bound thereby who did not consent to the alteration, any obligation, covenant or promise thereby undertaken or made. 

 A material alteration is one which varies the rights, liabilities, or legal position of the parties ascertained by the deed in its original state or otherwise varies the legal effect of the instrument as originally expressed, or reduces to certainty some provision which was originally unascertained and as such void, or may otherwise prejudice the party bound by the deed as originally executed. 

 44. From the materials on record, it appears to me that this is merely an allegation that the last sentence was an outcome of forgery but the respondent No.1 has failed to make out a case of forgery. I have given my anxious consideration on this last sentence as well as on the other parts of the agreement and it appear to me that it is very much consistent with the other parts, and the element of forgery is totally absent. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record I am of the view that the petitioners have been able to make out their case and as such they are entitled to have the relief as prayed for in the application.

parties:
Md. Badruddin Moral and others ------ Appellants
VS.
Santosh Kumar Sen and others ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
A.T.M. Afzal, J:- This is a plaintiffs' appeal by leave, The question raised is whether the High Court Division was justified in summarily rejecting the appellant's revisional application against the order of the Munsif, DebhataUpazila in Title Suit No. 8 of 1985 refusing permission to withdraw the said suit with liberty to sue afresh under Order XXIII, rule I (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 2. The aforesaid suit was originally instituted in the court of Munsif, Saikhira being Title Suit, No. 143 of 1973 and on transfer to DcbhaiaUpazila it was renumbered Title Suit No. HISS. The suit was for declaration of Title and further that the S.A. Khatian was wrong. Some of the defendants filed written statement r .sing, amongst others, the plea of res-judicata.

parties:
Juran Chandra Mondal
Vs.
Rabindra Nath Mondal
full_judgment:
2. The petitioners have filed Title suit No. 115 of 1974 in the Court of Munsif Gopalganj against the opposite party and others for a declaration of their title and confirmation of possession in respect of the suit land and the said suit was decreed exparte of 9-3-82. Thereafter the opposite party who was defendant No.3 in the suit filed on application under order 9 Rule 13 C.P.C. which was registered as Misc. case no.37 of 1983 for seating aside the exparte decree on the ground inter alia that no summons or registered letter was served upon him and that the services return has been shown as duly served in collusion with the process server. The opposite party came to know about the exparte decree on 30-3-83 when petitioner No.1 disclosed about the exparte decree. Thereafter the opposite party made a search in the court and got information about the date of his knowledge. 

 4. Mr. Shahid Alam, the learned Advocate appearing in support of the rule contends that the learned Munsif compared the signature of the opposite party in the service return with his, signatures take in the courts and found that both the signatures tally. The learned Munsif also observed that the opposite party and defendant No. 4 reside in the same homestead and as such the opposite party should have knowledge about the exparte-decree earlier than the date mentioned by him. Yet the learned Munsif allowed the Misc. case being of the opinion that the opposite party should get a chance to contest the original suit to prove his title to the suit land. According to Mr. Alam, the learned Munsif virtually found that summons was duly served upon the opposite party and as such the learned Munsif erred in law in allowing an application under order 9. Rule 13 C.P.C. and setting aside the exparte decree. Mr. Bazlur Rahman Talukdar, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party, on the other hand submits that the opposite party as P.W. 1 stated that he had no knowledge of the original suit and that no summons was served upon him. He has also examined as P.W. 2 Dhirendra Nath Barrio who has stated that he did not sign the alleged service return. On the other hand, the plaintiff opposite party adduced no evidence to prove that summons was duly served upon the opposite party. According to Mr. Talukdar the learned Munsif should have found on the evidence on record that no summons was served upon the opposite party. This being a case of non-service of summons the learned Munsif was justified in setting aside the exparte decree. In support of his contention Mr. Talukdar has referred to the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Md. Abdur Rashid and another V. Abdul Barik and another reported in 1984 B.L.D). (A.D.) 83. 

 5. It appears that although the learned Munsif compared the signature in the service return with the signature of P.W. 1 taken in the court he has not come to a definite finding that there was service of summons. On the other hand P.W. 1 stated that there was no service of summons upon him and that he had no knowledge of the original suit prior to the date of his knowledge as given in his application under order 9. Rule 13 C.P.C. P.W. 2 Dhirerndra Nath Barui has also stated that he did not sing the service return Ext.1 as witness. As regards the evidence adduced on behalf of the plaintiffs opposite parties, the learned Munsif found "The O.P. did not take any step to prove the service retain by adducing any evidence. O.P.1 as O.P.W. 1 has told that the process server of Ext.1 is dead. He could bring any other process server who knows the handwriting of Abdus Sattar who served the summons Ext. 1" Thus It appears that the plaintiffs opposite parties failed to prove by adducing cogent evidence that summons of the original suit was served upon opposite party defendant No.3. In that view of the matter, the irresistible conclusion is that there was no service of summons upon defendant No.3 and as such the exparte decree is liable to be set aside. In view of the decision of the Appellate Division referred to above that under order 9. Rule 13 C.P.C. if summons is not Duly served on the defendants that in a good ground for setting aside the exparte decree because service of summons is an essential condition which must be satisfied before the court can proceed to an exparte decree and when a party satisfies the court that summons were not duly served upon him the Court is bound to set aside the exparte decree. In such a case the question of knowledge is not at all relevant and the expert decree will be set aside even if the defendant had knowledge of the institution of the suit. In view of the finding that there was no service of summons the contention of Mr. Shahid Alam that the learned Munsif was wrong in allowing the application on compassionate ground to give a chance to the defendant to contest the suit need not be considered. In that view of the matter, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

parties:
Hasmat ------Petitioner
Vs.
Mofizuddin Majhi & ors------Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree, dated 30.12.81, passed by the Additional District. Judge, 3rd Court, Barisal in title Appeal No. 241 of 1977 affirming those, dated 22.9.77, passed by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Barisal in Title Suit No. 22 of 1972. 

 2. The plaintiff-petitioner and the defendant No. 22 who was originally plaintiff No. 2 filed Title Suit No. 22 of 1977 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal impleading the opposite parties and defendants for declaration that the compromise decree, dated 16.4.70 passed in Title Suit No. 109 of 1970 of the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal, was fraudulent, collusive, void and not binding upon the plaintiff and that the auction sale held on 21.12 62 in Certificate case No. 60/61.62 was fraudulent, collusive, and ineffective with regard to the plaintiff's title to the suit land . 

 3. The plaintiff's case, inter alia, was that the suit land in the 'Ka' schedule of the plaint originally belonged to Ushabala Chakraborty the defendant No. 15. The plaintiff, Hashem Ali and his brother Kashem Ali the pro-defendant No. 22 took settlement of the suit land from the said owner, the defendant No. 15. in Baisakh, 1349 B.S. and since then they have been in possession of the same by exercising their title therein. The defendant Nos. 1-21 have got no title and possession of the suit land. But the defendant Nos, 1-7 instituted Title Suit No. 109 of 1970 against the defendant Nos. 8 21 on the false allegations in respect of the suit land & other lands. in that suit the defendant No. 1 claimed title over the suit land on the basis of (Pattan allegedly taken from the defendant No. 15 in. 1354 B.S. and on the basis of auction purchase held in .Certificate Case No. 60K/61-62. But as a matter of fact defendant No. 1 never took pattan of any land from the defendant No. 15 who left this country for India for good in 1349 B.S. No summonses were served upon the defendant in that suit All these were collusively and fraudulently suppressed No notice or sale proclamation was ever served or issued in the Certificate Case. The sale held in the certificate case was fraudulent and collusive. The defendant managed to obtain a sole decree, dated 16.4.70 in the said Title Suit No. 109 of 1970 by practicing fraud upon the court. The Solenama filed in that suit is a forged document the defendant No. 15 never appeared and effected any compromise. Neither the plaintiff nor his brother, the defendant No. 22, was made a party in that suit. The plaintiff came to know about the same in Chitra, 1378 B S. while the defendant No. 1 claimed title over the suit land on the basis of the said illegal sole decree. 

 4. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filling a written statement. His case in brief was that he took settlement of the land of S.A. Khatian Nos. 165, 167 and 168 from the defendant no.15, Ushabala Chakraborty in Baisakh, 1354 B S. and since then he has been possessing the same. He auction purchased the lands of S. A. Khatian No. 169 on 21. 12. 62 in Certificate Case No. 60/ K 1961 62 and thereafter took possession of the same through Court and since then he has been in possession of the same. Thus the defendant No.1 is the owner and possessor of the suit land. The sole decree, dated 16.4 70 passed in Title Suit No. 109 of 1970 and the auction sale held on 21. 12. 62 on Certificate Case No. 60K/ 61-e2 are quite legal and valid. The notices and the sale proclamation were duly issued and served in the Certificate Case. The summons were also duly served upon the defendants of Title Suit No. 109 of 1970. The defendants of the suit duly signed the solenama which is a genuine document. The plaintiff and his brother, the defendant No 22, never acquired any title or possession in the suit land. The suit is not maintainable in the present form. The plaintiff has no locus-stand to file the suit; the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 5. On consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record, the trial court, dismissed the suit with the finding that the plaintiff has got neither title nor possession in the suit property; that the plaintiff has no locus standi to fife the suit and that the suit is not maintainable and it is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The trial court further found that the plaintiff has failed to establish that the impugned decree and Certificate sale were illegal, collusive, fraudulent and void. 

 6. The plaintiff-petitioner being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree preferred Title Appeal No. 241 of 1977 which was also dismissed by the Additional District Judge 3rd Court, Barisal. On consideration of evidence on record the appellate court recorded the following finding:-'As the plaintiff has got no title or possession in the suit laud and as he has not made any prayer in this suit for declaration of title and for any consequential relief either in the Arm confirmation of possession or recovery of khas possession so it can be safely said that the plaintiff has got no locus-standi to bring the suit and that suit is nor maintainable in its present form" Being aggrieved by the aforesaid decision of the appellate Court, the plaintiff petitioner moved a revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule. 

 8. Mr. Md. Nizamul Huq, the learned Advocate for the petitioner contended that though the plaintiff has failed to prove his right, title and interest in the suit land, yet he is entitled to a part decree as the defendant has failed to prove that the compromise decree, dated 16.4.70 passed in Title Suit No.109 of 1970 was a genuine document. 

 10. The present suit. is a suit for Sinters declaration and was filed under the provision of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, which runs as follow-"Any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to the property, may institute a suit against any persons denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the court may in its discretion, make therein a declaration that be is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit seek for any further relief : Provided that no court, shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than mere declaration of title omits to do so. To maintain a suit under this section the following 2 ingredients must be proved :- (I) that plaintiff is entitled to a legal character or right as to the property. (I1) and that the defendant is denying or is interested to deny such character or right .So, the suit must fail if the plaintiff fails to establish his legal character or title which authorises him to ask for the declaratory decree. In the case of Mst. Sabera Khatunn Vs. Mst. Arnena Khatun reported in I SCR (i981) page 127 it has been held by a Division Bench of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court that :—"Before the plaintiff can be given a declaration under section 42, Specific Relief Act she has to prove before the Court that she had the legal character or the right to property she claimed and unless the plaintiff could prove such legal character or right to property she could not be given any declaratory relief." 

 11. The same view has been taken by another Division Bench of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court in the Case of Imanuddin. Parks' Vs. Lilabati Dos reported in 32 D.L R. page 75. Their Lordships of the Division Bench held as follows: — 11The plaintiff has prayed for a declaration to the effect that the decree obtained by the defendant was fraudulent arid collusive and not binding against the plaintiff. The plaintiff having failed to prove her title and having no legal character in the subject matter of the suit land, was not entitled to any declaration with regard to the defendant's decree to which she had not connection". 

 12. It is now an established principle of law that the plaintiff is to succeed on the merit of his own case and he having failed to prove his title in the suit property, the plain; tiff has no legal character and as, such he in not entitled to any declaration that the compromise decree obtained by the defendant is fraudulent, collusive, and null and void. 

 13. in the present case both the trial court and the appellate court have concurrently found that the plaintiff has failed to prove his title and possession of the suit property and as such he has no locus-standi to file the present suit which is not maintainable being hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. On consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case, evidence on record and the relevant laws, I hold that the plaintiff having no locus-standi to file the present suit, he is not entitled to any declaration against the defendant No. 1 with regard to compromise decree; dated I 6.4-70 passed in Title Suit No. 109 of 1970 and the suit has been rightly dismissed by the courts below. There is no force in the argument of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner.

parties:
Kalimuddin Saarder ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Assistant Custodian, Enemy Property and others ----- Opp. -Parties
full_judgment:
Anwarul Hoque Chowdhury, J. This revisional application is directed against the judgment and order dated 22.5.79 of the learned District Judge, Jessore passed in Title Appeal No. 149/78 confirming those passed by the learned Munsif in Title Suit No. 296/75 dismissing the suit. 

 Facts in short are that plaintiff filed a suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in the suit land, alleging inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to one Soku Mondal under landlord Nasiruddin Mondal. After Soku Mondal's death the landlord possessed it in khas when the superior interest was auction purchased by one Bibhuti Bhushan and he settled the same with the plaintiff in the year 1357 B.S. at rental of Tk. 5/- and since 1357 B.S. plaintiff had been possessing the suit land on payment of rent though the land was erroneously recorded in the names of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 who are the sons of the Bibhuti Bhushan when the custodian of enemy property declared the land as an enemy property. Hence the suit the suit was contested by defendant No. 3 who alleged that the land was correctly recorded in the name of the sons of Bibhuti Bhushan who are now Indian nationals since 1965 and hence the government considered the suit land as enemy property. The court of first instance dismissed the suit and the same was affirmed by the learned District Judge against which Kalimuddin Sarder has moved this application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and had obtained this Rule. 

 4. In the instant case the plaintiff claimed tenancy right in the suit land under Bibhuti Bushan and not under his sons whose names are subsequently recorded in the respective khatian and who were impleaded as defendants 1 and 2 in the suit by the plaintiff himself. The plaintiff in order to prove the settlement could not produce any documentary evidence, such as patta or kabulyat but Dakhilas of these nature, which are private documents would not carry with it any presumption of correctness as would be available in the case of an entry in the record of right under the provisions of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The said dakhilas thus need "to be proved, out of necessity by person who wishes the court to believe in the existence of these papers to the satisfaction of the court by any of the ways that would be considered by the Court of Law sufficient to prove a document as the Evidence Act does not provide any particular mode of proving a document. It can be proved by calling the scribe, and in case the signature of the executant was disputed, by comparing the disputed signature with other proved signature of the executant and by taking the opinion of a handwriting expert and in the case of a document need to be attested by examing at least one of the attesting witness. In the instant case the documents or dakhilas, when challenged by the opposite parties to be a concocted document, need be proved by producing the scribe as a witness and also the executant to prove that he had in fact signed the document as an employee under the Zamindar and had the authority granted by Landlord to grant such a receipt and finally by producing the counter-foil of those dakhilas. In the instant case nothing of that nature had been done. No counterfoil had been produced neither the scribe nor the executant deposed in favour of the dakhila. The Courts below on an examination of those documents found those to be of recent origin and therefore of no legal value. The question whether a document is a genuine document or not is essentially a question of fact and a finding of fact to that effect need not to be interfered with by this court in revisional jurisdiction unless it could be shown that the finding was not warranted by the evidence on record which would give rise to a question of legality. In the instant case the finding of fact to the effect that the documents were of recent origin and that the plaintiff could not prove his title to the suit land by other document of title, do not seem to have been arrived at by causing any error of law or which was not warranted by the evidence on record. Hence the contention of the learned Advocate that the court below committed an error in this regard cannot be sustained. 

 5. Mr. Abdur Rahim has next contended that the courts did not consider the plaintiff's claim of adverse possession though it was the plaintiff's specific case. On a reference to the records it is seen that the plaintiff did state so in his plaint claiming title by adverse possession and also by means of settlement which appears to be inconsistent statements. But under the law a party can take inconsistent pleas but on a reference to the judgment of the trial court it is seen that no such issue as to adverse possession had been framed at the trial nor the parties fought out the suit on such an issue and that being position the same could not be allowed now at this stage in revisional jurisdiction before this court to be agitated as neither issue were framed in this regard nor evidence led to that effect. 

 6. Mr. Abdur Rahim has also urged as to possession of the plaintiff and had taken pains in taking me through the evidence on record to show that there existed evidence on record to show that the plaintiff was in possession since 1357 B.S. corresponding to 1950 A.D. This question of possession would be irrelevant in the facts and circumstances of the case as plaintiff's possession must be referable either to the settlement or possession adversely and the claim of adverse possession having been abandoned at the trial the question of settlement would be the only point that remained and the said also could not be proved by the plaintiff to the satisfaction of the Court. A mere possession would not create title further when the said claim contradicts the entry in the names of the sons of the landlords in the khatian respecting the land in question as an entry in the khatian is also evidence of possession. No other points urged. All having been found against the petitioner I find no substance in this revisional application.

caseno: Appeal from original Decree No. 165 of 1965
parties:
Imanuddin Rarhi ----- Appellant in F A No 169 and Respondent in F.A. No. 165/65.
Vs.
Lilabati Das ----- Respondent in F.A. 169 and Appellant in F.A. No. 165/65.
full_judgment:
Abdul Wadud Chowdhury J: These two appeals are directed against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Barisal dated 23-1-1965 in Title Suit No. 367 of 1963 and arises out of a suit for declaration of the plaintiff's raiyat right in Kha schedule land as also for a further declaration that the ex-parte decree that was passed in Title Suit No. 449 of 1961 of the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge. Barisal, detailed in schedule 'Ka' of the plaint is void, inoperative and not binding upon the plaintiff. 

 2. The Plaintiff's case to the effect that the suit properties described in 'Kha' schedule of the plaint was acquired by the plaintiff in the benami of Sudhendu Roy Chowdhury and Serala Sundari Basu by virtue of two pattas and Kabalas of different dates. The Plaintiff, however, took settlement of the suit land from Sudhendu Nath Roy Chowdhury by a patta dated 22nd Jaistha, 1348 BS corresponding to 5-9-35 AD in the name of Serala Sundari Basu. She paid selami of Rs. 475 for the patta. The plaintiff again took settlement of land from Sarala Sundari Basu in the benami of Sudhendu Nath Roy Chowdhury by a patta dated 19th Kartick, 1360 BS (5-11-53) and she paid the selami for the same. Both the pattas were in the custody of the plaintiff. After the said pattas Sarala Sundari sold her superior right to" the Plaintiff by a kabala dated 21st Kartick, 1360 BS (7-11-53) and the said kabala was taken in the benami of Sudhendu Nath Roy. Consideration money was paid by the Plaintiff. As such three documents were executed in the benami of Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari with the money and in the interest of the Plaintiff and Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari were mere name lenders of the Plaintiff being near relations of her. The Plaintiff thus acquired the suit property in the benami of Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari Basu. During the RS operation the suit properties were recorded in the name of the said two benamders at her instance. Subsequently since Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari did not execute any Nadabi Patia, she brought Title Suit No. 267 of 1960 before the Court of the Sub-ordinate Judge, Barisal for declaration of her title with respect to the disputed properties and obtained an ex-parte decree on 2-9-60. Thereafter, the Plaintiff got her name mutated in place of those persons before the acquired Estate and the name of the benamders were struck off from the settlement record. The Plaintiff later on came to know from her husband that the defendant obtained a decree in respect of 'Kha' schedule land in Title Suit No. 449 of 1961 of the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Barisal on 9-3-65 although the defendant No. 1 had no right, title or possession in the suit property. No summons of the said suit was served either on Sudhendu Nath Roy or Sarala Sundari Basu as those two persons were Indian citizens. As such, the alleged ex-parte decree is fraudulent and not binding on the plaintiff. The defendant No. 1 got the summons of the said suit served on one Mafizuddin alleging him to be Karmachari of Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari Basu though he was not so. The defendant has no title or possession in the suit properties and the story of settlement from Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari is false. There was no settlement of the suit properties by Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari in favour of defendant No. 1 and no possession was delivered to the defendant No. by them. As such the defendants did not acquire any title to the suit property by virtue of the said decree which is fraudulent. The plaintiff acquired right, title and interest in the suit property by virtue of her pattas and kabala and subsequently by virtue of her ex-parte decree obtained against Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari. In that view of the matter, the plaintiff has filed the present suit for declaration as above as a cloud has been cast upon the title of the plaintiff. 

 3. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit contending, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable in its present form the plaintiff's story of acquiring of title on the basis, of said pattas and the Kabalas are denied by the defendant No. 1. He further contended that the said three documents were not benami transactions and neither Sudhendu Nath Roy nor Sarala Sundari was the benamider of the plaintiff. No consideration did pass at the instance of the plaintiff herself with regard to the said three documents. It was further contended by the Defendant that the plaintiff was never in possession of the suit properties and she acquired no title in the same as benamder of Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari. The defendant further contended that Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari acquired the suit properties in their own names with their own modify and the RS records were correctly prepared in their names. While thus in possession on the owners i.e. Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari settled the suit property with the defendants on 28th Chaitra 1360 BS at a jama of Rs. 15 and delivered possession to him. The defendant No. 1 is in possession of the suit land since the settlement in his favour. As SA Khatian did not record the name of the defendant in spite of his settlement he brought Title Suit No. 449 of 1961 before the court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Barisal against Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari and obtained a decree after due service of summons upon the said two persons. The said decree was bonafide and could not be called into question by the plaintiff. As Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari leased out the suit property to the defendant No. 1, the husband of the plaintiff subsequently obtained the original pattas and kabala clandestinely and brought Title Suit No; 267 of 1960 and obtained a fraudulent decree against Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari in respect of the suit property. Neither the plaintiff nor her husband ever posseted the suit property or realised any rent from tenants. The defendant further contended that the decree obtained by the defendant against Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari was bonafide and valid decree after due service of summons upon them at their Barisal residence. The husband of the plaintiff is the proprietor of the Sonali Cinema Hall. His business is to acquire properties of thereon resident Hindus and to prepare false and forged documents in his name from the aforesaid non-resident Hindus. It was further staged that the suit of the Plaintiff is hit by Ordinances I and VI of 1964 and the Plaintiff has no locus standi or any legal character to file the present suit. 

 4. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge dismissed the suit of the Plaintiff holding that the plaintiff could not prove her title by benami purchase in the name of Sudhendu Nath Roy and Sarala Sundari. He found that the ingredients of benami have not been proved. He also found that the plaintiff's ex-parte decree in Title Suit No. 267 of 1960, the sheet anchor of the plaintiff's title, was tinged with fraud in view of the fact that though the defendants of that suit i.e. Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari were not in the then Pakistan and were Indian citizen yet notices were served upon them at Barisal through one Daruba Nath PW 3. Though Daruba Nath has admitted that he had no interest in the suit proper-ties yet he was made a defendant in the said suit. In that view of the matter, he found that the plaintiff did not acquire the suit properties in the benami of Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari. He also found that the decree obtained by the plaintiff in the Title Suit No 267 of 1960 against Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari. In respect of the suit properties is nothing but fraudulent and, as such, the plaintiff has got no title in the 'Kha' schedule properties and the case of benami has not been proved. He has, however, found that the plaintiff has proved his present possession from the time of the ex-parte decree obtained by him. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge after deciding that the plaintiff has no title or interest in the suit land and that the ex-parte decree obtained by him against Sudhendu Nath and Sarala were fraudulent, also considered the decrees obtained by the defendant No. 1 was also fraudulent and collusive as such he dismissed the suit of the plaintiff with the finding that the ex-parte decree passed in Title Suit Nos. 449 of 1961 and 267 of 1960 of that court was also declared to be null and void. As against the said judgment and decree passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, both the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 preferred two appeals. The plaintiff's appeal is FA No. 169 of 1965 and the defendant's appeal is FA No. 165 of 1965. The Plaintiff's appeal was against the dismissal of his case as also against the declaration that his ex-parte decree in Title Suit No. 267 of 1960 was fraudulent and null and void. The delft's appeal was against the findings of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge that the Title Suit No. 449 of 1061 obtained by him against Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari was fraudulent and, as such, null and void. As these two appeals arise out of the same judgment and decree and is with regard to the same suit land we dispose of both these appeals by this judgment. 

 5. Mr Anil Chandra Sarkar appeared on behalf of the plaintiff appellant in FA No. 169 of 1965 and Mr. Nizamuddin Haider with Mr. ABM Abbasuddin appeared on behalf of the defendant No. 1 appellant in FA No. 165 of 1965. Mr Anil Chandra Sarker learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the Plaintiff appellant in FA No. 169 of 1965, submits that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge erred in law and against the weight of evidence on record in holding that the plaintiff has not been able to-prove her title by benami purchase. He then submits that the trial court should not have decided the propriety or otherwise of the ex-parte decree passed in favour of the plaintiff in Title, Suit No. 267 of 1960 in view of the fact that no specific issue has been raised as regard the said decree and no particulars of fraud have been alleged in the written statement and no evidence of fraud have been given by the defendant. He further submits that the said ex parte decree ought to have been accepted by the court below as valid. He also submits that the benami character of the suit land cannot be set-aside without setting aside the ex-parte decree and the ex-parte decree cannot be act aside at the instance of the defendant No. 1 who could not challenge it because he was not a party to the said suit Mr Sarkar learned Advocate further urged that in view of the finding of possession arrived at by the trial court he is entitled to a declaration to the effect that the defendant's decree was fraudulent and void. Mr Nizamuddin Haider the learned Advocate, on the other hand, submits that the trial court's findings so far as the question of benami and declaration to the effect that the plaintiffs ex parte decree was fraudulent are based on sound principle of law and should be maintained but so far as the decree declaring the defendant's decree in Title Suit No. 449 of 1961, to be fraudulent and null and void is not maintainable in view of the fact that the plaintiff is to succeed on his own case and she having failed to prove her title in the suit property. She has no legal character and as such she is not entitled to any such declaration that the decree obtained by the defendant was forged, null and void. As regards the first point urged by Mr Sarker that he has been able to prove benami character of the said documents. We find from the judgment of the court below that he has considered about the benami character of those documents. He has found out that the plaintiff had no relationship with Sudhendu Nath & Sarala Sundari. He also found that there is no evidence of payment by the plaintiff of the consideration money. As regards the custody of the document the learned Sub-ordinate Judge has found that those documents came into possession of the plaintiff in connection with the purchase of land from a co-sharers of Sudhendu Nath i.e. Defendant No. 2, Jatindra Nath Roy the brother of Sudhendu Nath Roy. He also found that that the Plaintiff could not prove any motive for the said alleged benami transactions. We have considered the evidence on record; we do not find that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge has committed any error in coming to such finding. We also, on consideration of evidence on record, find that the plaintiff has not been able to prove the ingredients of benami. In that view of the matter the learned sub-ordinate Judge was correct in holding that the plaintiff had no right, title and interest in the suit land. In the light of the said finding it was necessary for the court to come into the question as to how the ex-parte decree was obtained by the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 267 of 1960. The plaintiff claimed title, by virtue of benami purchase and the ex-parte decree. The ex-parte decree was obtained on the basis of the benami. So when it has been found that the plaintiff could not prove benami character of the transacting it could not be said that the ex-parte decree has any leg to stand upon. In order to find out whether the plaintiff had any right, title and interest in the suit land, the consideration as to whether the said-decree was validly obtained or not was necessary. It cannot be said that since the decree has been passed in Title Suit No. 267 of 1960 the court cannot go into the question of the validity of the decree. In order to arrive at a finding as to whether the Plaintiff had any right, title or interest in the kha schedule property the court has of necessity to go into the question of the question of the genuineness of the ex-parte decree and to Come to a finding whether the same was a valid decree or not. In that view of the matter the objection taken by the learned Advocate for the appellant that since no issue has been raised on the quest ion of validity of the said ex-parte decree the same could not be considered by the trial count and the decree cannot be set aside. We are unable or accept the said contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant. The court was within his province in sifting the evidence or record as to whether the ex-parte decree was genuine or tinged with fraud. It is of no consequence whether the defendant raised any objection with regard to the said ex-parte decree. The Plaintiff was to prove her case and in proving heir case she has to adduce evidence as to whether the said decree which was the sheet-anchor of her title was valid or not. When the court on consideration of the facts, circumstances and evidence led in the case came to the conclusion that the transfers were genuine and not benami and the plaintiff did not acquire the property in the benami of Sudhendra Nath and Sarala Sundari, obviously it has to see whether the ex-parte decree obtained on the basis of the said allegation of benami has legs to stand upon. So we do not find any illegality in the findings of the learned Sub-ordinate Judge in considering the genuineness of the ex-parte decree. In that view of the matter we do not find any sub-stance in the argument advanced by the learned Advocate for the appellant that the decree could not be assailed or set-aside by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge in the present suit. Moreover, the evidence on record discussed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge as discussed in the judgment tends to show that the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 267 of 1960 was fraudulently obtained because of the fact that though there is evidence on record to the effect that Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari were Indian citizens and were not living in the then East Pakistan for a long time, curiously enough the summons were served on them at Barisal through PW 3 Daruba Nath. This Dhruba Nath was made party in that suit though he admitted in his deposition here that he had no interest whatsoever in the suit land and Dhruba Nath PW 3 was an employee of the husband of the plaintiff. This alone is enough to come to a finding that the decree was fraudulent. It has been argued by Mr Sarkar, the learned Advocate that since no fraud has been alleged by the defendant the court suo motu could not go into that question and set-aside the decree. But as we have stated earlier, the genuineness or otherwise of the said decree was very much in issue in deciding the title of the plaintiff as it was found that the plaintiff could not prove benami character-of the documents. In that view the nature and character of the ex-parte decree required scrutiny and the court on scrutinising the same has found that the said decree was obtained fraudulently. We do not find any illegality in the treatment of the case by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge on this account. 

 6. Mr Sarker, the learned Advocate for the appellant has further submitted that in view of the fact that the court has found possession of the suit land with the plaintiff he had a legal character and he was entitled to a declaration that the defendant's decree was fraudulent and null and void. Let us now examine section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is as follows:— 

 "Any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the court may in its discretion make therein a declaration that he is so entitled and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief; Provided that no court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so" 

 7. The Plaintiff may ask for relief under that section provided that the plaintiff must at the time of the suit be entitled to any legal character or to any right to any property. Section 42 must be construed strictly. The courts are only to grant such declaration which came within the terms of that section where the plaintiff has asked for a declaratory decree, namely a declaration that the decree obtained was fraudulent and void. Such a simple declaration could not be given within the provisions; of section 42 as such the suit on the face of that section has to be dismissed. In the present case we find that the plaintiff could not prove her title to the suit land although the learned Sub-ordinate Judge has found that he was in possession of the same since the passing of the ex-parte decree in his favour. Mr Sarker, the Learned Advocate has referred to a decision of this court in the case of Aminul Islam vs M/s Kilburn & Co. reported in 18 DLR 691 where it has been held that if a possessor owner is wrongfully deprived of the thing by person other than the true owner he can recover khas possession of it, after evicting the defendant from the land on the basis of possessory title even if he has not acquired any valid title. The facts of that case are completely different from the present case. In the reported case the suit was filed under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act on the averment that the plaintiff was in possession and he has been subsequently dispossessed from the suit land on encroachment by the defendant. There it was held that thought the plaintiff did not acquire any valid title, he was entitled to recover khas possession. Of course, in that case the plaintiff acquired goodwill and all interest of the original owner by virtue of an agreement. In the agreement it was stated that consideration of the goodwill and the assets of the original owner passed to the plaintiff and he would be paid by allotment of shares. In consequence of that transaction they were in possession of the suit land. It was found that the original Company validly transferred the disputed land to the plaintiff till they were dispossessed by the defendant. It was found there that the plaintiff did not acquire valid title to the suit land as no instrument of transfer was effected between the plaintiff and the original owner. But in the context it was held that plaintiff was entitled to a decree for khas possession. But in the present case the plaintiff did not file any suit for khas possession or anything of that sort and there is also nothing to show that the owners of the land transferred the suit land in favour of the plaintiff. But on the other hand, it has been found by the court below as also by us that the plaintiff could riot prove the benami nature of the document. Rather the findings of the court below are to the effect that the plaintiff went into possession of the suit land after the passing of the ex-parte decree. In that view of the matter, the decision cited by Mr Sarker is of assistance to this case. The Plaintiff has prayed for a declaration to the effect that the decree obtained by the defendant was fraudulent and collusive and not binding against the plaintiff. The plaintiff having failed to prove her title and having no legal character in the subject matter of the suit land, was not entitled to any declaration with regard to the defendant's decree to which she had no connection. If however, it transpires from the evidence on record that the decree obtained by the defendant was also tainted with the same defect as that of the plaintiff though in the present suit. We do not hold that the plaintiff was entitled of any such declaration with regard to the defendant's decree since the matter is not before us. In the interest of justice we notice that the defendant No. 1's decree was also not in accordance with law, Summons of the suit was served on a person who had no interest in the suit and admittedly the defendants of that suit were Indian citizens, but their addresses in the suit were given to be in East Pakistan. From all these the learned Sub-ordinate Judge was correct in holding that the defendant's decree also suffers from the same defect as that of the Plaintiff. However, since the plaintiff has no locus standi to challenge the same and Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari were not parties in the present suit we do not declare in the present suit the defendant's decree to be a nullify. Another factor to be noticed in the present case was that Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari were impleaded as deft. Nos. 2 and 3 in the present suit but ultimately their names were struck off. The title to the suit land remained with Sudhendu Nath and Sarala Sundari, as such, they having not been implicated, their names having been struck off; the learned Sub-ordinate Judge has correctly dismissed the suit holding that the present suit was not maintainable in the absence of the real owners.

parties:
Hiralal Agarwala ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
Deputy Commr. Bogra & ors ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
3. The case of the petitioner is that he has got both right and title as well as possession in the 8 annas share of the entire property including land and business and this share was never an enemy property to vest in the Government. The impugned order and action of the Government, as stated above, are without lawful authority and malafide. 

 4. The respondent, Government of Bangladesh, contested the Rule by filing affidavit in opposition denying altogether the petitioner's claim of ownership and title in the 8 annex of the property including the Rice Mill. Their contention is that Parallax Agarwala who had 8 annals share in the property was a lift long bachelor and he went to India before 1965 whereupon his 8 annas share in the property automatically became an enemy property which ultimately vested in the Government; the petitioners got no right, title at all in this 8 annas share of Prahallad Agarwala. As to the business under the name and style Sree Balajee Rice Mill, the contention of respondents is that the Rice Mill also belonged to Prahallad Agarwala in which the petitioner did not contribute anything but he was simply a partner in the business with Prallad's co-sharer Hariram Agarwala. Both the Rice Mill and Land in respect of 8 annas share having become enemy property ultimately vesting in the Government the impugned order of the respondent Government is perfectly wrongful and there is malafide in it. Further contention of the respondent is that the petitioner took resort to falsehood by setting up one Laxmi Devi respondent No. 4 widow of Prahallad Agarwala whereas Prahallad Agarwala died bachelor ; in the said O.C. Suit No. 232 of 1977 which was filed by the petitioner along with the said Laxmi Devi praying for declaration of their title to the 8 annas share of property it was withdrawn by them when a written statement was filed by the respondents disclosing the real facts and when the Civil Suit for title was withdrawn, the petitioner is not entitled to the remedy under writ jurisdiction as an order under Article 102 of the Constitution in this case would amount to declaration of the petitioner title which had failed to be proved in the Civil Court. 

 7. Now coming to the other petition, petition No. 609 of 1977 we have heard Mr. M, Golam Rabbani, the learned Advocate for the petitioner and Mr. M. M. Huq, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing for the respondent Government. The facts which are not disputed in this case are that Prahallad Agarwala and Hariram Agarwala were the recorded owners of the land measuring 5.31 acre in equal shares. Petitioner's claim that he got some share in the 8 annas share of his uncle Prahallad Agarwala has no basis or any evidence except his oral claim. As such this claim cannot be accepted and it is, therefore, found that Prahallad Agarwala was the owner of the 8 annas share of this land. As to Prahallad Agarwala there is also no basis of the petitioner's claim that Prahallad Agarwala remained in India and thereafter in Bangladesh till 1971. On the other hand, the contention of the respondent is that Prahallad Agarwala went over to India before 1965 where he died appears to be borne out by facts as such he was an enemy alien and in his absence his share of the property became an enemy property under the Defence of Pakistan Rules and thereafter it vested in the Government.
