The petitioner along with one Laxmi Devi filed a Title Suit No. 232 of 1977 for declaration of their title to 8 annas share of the property left by Prahallad Agarwala but the suit was ultimately withdrawn. We need, not discuss whether Prahallad Aagrwala had left any widow or he died a bachelor put since Laxmi Devi respondent No. 4 is not coming before us claiming to be an heir of Prahallad Agarwala the petitioner's claim is to be rejected outright. But the case of the petitioner is that even if he got no right, title in the 8 annas share of Prahallad Agarwala he got right, title as well as possession in the 8 annas share of the business under name and style Sree Balajee Rice Mill which was set up under registered partnership deed dated 31.12.58 and as such this 11 annas share in the business Which never belonged to Prahallad Agarwala is not an Enemy Property and never vested in the Government. Mr M. M. Huq does not dispute the partnership deed, Annexure A dated 30.12.58 does not challenge this partnership deed which is a registered one. But his contention is that this relates to a partnership in the businesses between the petitioner and Hariram Agarwala but the petitioner did not contribute any capital and since the Rice Mill was set up in the land which belonged to Prahallad Agarwala and his co-sharer Hariram Agarwala it is presumed that the Mill belonged to these 2 co-sharers. But recital in the partnership deed does not support Mr. Huq since there is nothing mentioned in it as to what would be the relation between the petitioner Hiralal Agarwala and his uncle Prahallad Agarwala in respect of the Rice Mill. It is true that the land on which the Rice Mill was set up did not belong to the petitioner. But his partnership deed also does not say anything whether the petitioner, one of the 2 partners in the business, would be treated as a licensee or lessee in respect of the portion of the land covered by Rice Mill. The partnership deed simply shows that the 2 partners, Hiralal Agarwala and Hariram Agarwala, would have equal share in the business profits. Mr. Huq contends that at least this recital shows that the petitioner did not contribute any-thing to the capital of the business. Similarly it does not also show that Prahallad contributed anything by way of capital either. That Prahallad Agarwala was 8 annas owner in respect of the land does not necessarily show that he had contributed the 50% of the Rice Mill and started business. Unless it is shown that 8 annas share in the business and the Rice Mill belonged to Prahallad Agarwala this 8 annas share could not have been treated as Enemy Property. Admittedly, the petitioner has been in joint possession and control as well as management of this business since 1958 along with his partner Hariram Agarwala and if the land did not belong to him he could not be treated as trespasser either, for when he entered into the land for the purpose of business he was certainly authorised by the other owner, namely, Prahallad. That without approval he could not have become a partner in the business in that land. Mr Huq has stressed that there is no evidence to show that the petitioner got any share in the capital. The petitioner may not have any share in the capital but he has certainly got 8 annas share in the business property and this interest in the business cannot be affected by the declaration of the property i.e. the land is vested property. Mr. Rabbani has submitted that there is no disturbance at all so Iong the petitioners original business partner Hariram Agarwala is there. But disturbance started when respondent No. 5 Mokabbar purchased the 8 annas share of Hariram Agarwala. It further appears that respondent No. 5 also entered into a partnership under registered partnership deed dated 5.2.75 with the petitioner. That had 8 annas share in possession of the  petitioner been an Enemy Properly and subsequently vested then respondent No. 5 would not have entered such partnership business. From this fact it is clear that it is respondent No. 5 Mokabbar Hossain who manipulated everything in the matter so as to oust the petitioner from his share in the business. The impugned order dated 28.8.76 so far as it affected the petitioner's right in the Rice Mill and business is found to be without any lawful authority no matter the petitioner got no right, title in the land which originally belonged to Prahallad Agarwala and now vested in the Government.

caseno: Appeal From Appellate Decree No. 245 of 1964.
parties:
Abbas Sheikh & another ------ Defendant-Appellants. 
Vs. 
Md. Abu Hossain Sarkar and others ------Plaintiffs-Respondents.
full_judgment:
This appeal at the instance of the defendants is directed against the judgment of the lower appellate court affirming the judgment of the trial court decreeing the plaintiff's suit for declaration of title and confirmation of the possession of the disputed suit land. According to the plaintiffs the disputed jot belonged to one Kasimuddin and Imaruddin being two brothers. Imaruddin died leaving a sister and Kasimuddin. Then Kasimuddin died leaving his widow, two sons and a daughter. Then one of the sons of Kasimuddin i.e. Nurul Huq died unmarried leaving his mother, brother and sister as his heirs. One Ayenuddin predecessor of the Plaintiff Nos. 1 to 8 took settlement of the jot by a registered patta. Since the settlement Ayenuddin allegedly possessed the suit land and after his death his heirs i.e. plaintiffs had been in possession thereof within the knowledge of the defendants. The defendants No. 9 and 10 took usufructuary mortgage of the suit land from the rest of the plaintiffs and they were in possession thereof having been threatened with dispossession by the defendants, the present suit was instituted at the instance of the plaintiff for declaration of title and confirmation of possession of the suit land. 

 3. On consideration of the evidence on record both the courts below came to a concurrent finding of fact that the plaintiffs had acquired right, title and interest in the suit land by dint of the patta executed in favour of Ayenuddin by the sister of Imaruddin and widow of Kasimuddin who had also executed the patta on behalf on her two minor sons i.e, the present contesting defendant No. 1 and 6. With regard to the patta in question both the courts below came to a concurrent finding that by dint of the said patta the right title and interest of the sister of Imaruddin and the widow of the Kasimuddin had passed to Ayenuddin, but both the courts below also came to a concurrent finding that when the said patta was executed, minor children and on their behalf their mother i.e. the widow of Kasimuddin had executed the patta in question The court below also came to a concurrent finding that although the patta in question was partly void with regard to the right, title and interest of the defendants No. 1 and 6 since they were minors at the time of the execution of the patta and since their mother had no authority to execute the said patta on behalf of her minor children, but the plaintiffs having remained in possession of the suit land for more than 12 years, acquired right, title and interest therein by adverse possession thereof. 

 4. This case is otherwise concluded by a concurrent finding with regard to the plaintiffs' title in the suit land by dint of the patta executed in favour of the plaintiffs predecessor by the mother and aunt of contesting defendants. The only question of law raised in this case is as to whether the plaintiffs had acquired any right, title and interest in the suit land as against contesting defendant No. 1 and 6 by adverse possession of the suit land from the date of the execution of the patta when evidently the contesting defendants were minors and their mother had no authority to execute the patta on their behalf. 

 5. The learned Advocate for the defendants appellants had submitted that there—cannot be any adverse possession as against the minors during the period of their minority unless such adverse possession is claimed from the date of the attainment of their majority. The learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-respondents has, however, submitted that the suit land being jointly owned by the contesting defendants No. 1 and 6 along with their mother and aunt and the patta having been executed by the aunt and the mother not only on their own behalf but also on behalf of the minor defendants and since the plaintiffs had been in possession of the entire suit land since then, it shall be deemed that the plaintiffs had acquired right, title and interest in the suit land by adverse possession thereof. 

 7. Under section 6 of the Limitation Act, where a person entitled to institute a suit, is a minor at the time from which the period of limitation is to be reckoned such person may institute the suit within the same period after the disability has ceased. Under Section 7 of the Limitation Act, where one of several persons jointly entitled to institute a suit is under any such disability, time will not run as against any of them until the disability has ceased. Under Section 8 of the Limitation Act, none of the provisions of section 6 and 7 of the Limitation Act shall be deemed to extend for more than 3 years from the cessation of the disability of the person affected thereby. Under section 28 of the Limitation Act, at the determination of the period of limitation for instituting a suit for possession of any property, the right to such property shall be extinguished. Under Article 44 of the Limitation Act, a suit by award who has attained majority to set aside the transfer of any property by his guardian, can be instituted within three years from the time when the ward attains majority. 

 8. Considering the aforesaid provisions of the Limitation Act it clearly appears that a minor's right to action against his adversary with regard to the transfer of any property during his minority arises only, when he attains majority and not before. The provisions of law referred to above relates to a minor acting as a plaintiff but do no relate to a minor acting as a defendant. But if the minor suffers from any disability for acting as the plaintiff, he is normally supposed to suffer from the said disability while acting as a defendant. If a minor is entitled to challenge any transaction relating to his property transferred by his guardian on his behalf during his minority, only on his attainment of majority, it normally follows that any action against a minor on account of such transaction with relation to such property transferred by his guardian during his minority; would only lie when such minor attains majority. In such circumstances as in the present case if the plaintiffs wanted to claim. adverse possession against the present defendants with regard to the suit land, that can only be claimed from the date of the attainment of majority by the defendants concerned and not from any time when they were in minority. It is, of course, evident that from the time of attain runt of majority by the contesting defendants concerned till the institution of the present suit, the plaintiffs were not in adverse possession of the suit land as such. 

 9. On this question various judicial decisions have been cited by the learned advocates. concerned. The learned Advocate for The appellants has cited 26 C. W. N. 65, A. I. .R 1940- (Cal.) 589 and A. I. R. 1941 (Sind) 50. The learned advocate for. the respondents has cited 3 D. L. R. 305, 5 D. L. R. 383,-7 D. L. R.. 04, and 21 D. L. R. (S.C.) 444. So far as the decisions. referred to in 3 D. L. R. 5 D. L. R. and 7 D. L. R. are concerned, in these cases, the actions were taken at the instance of the minors on their attainment of majority and these decisions do not relate to a case where actions were taken against the miners as such. Thus, the said decisions are not applicable in the facts of this case. So far as a Division Bench Judgment by A. Sattar and M. R. Khan, JJ. of the Supreme Court of Pakistan reported in 21 D. L. R. (S.C.) 444 is concerned, it appears that in this case action was taken against the minors on their attainment of majority. In the said case adverse possession claimed against the defendants was allowed although the defendants properly was transferred during their minority, on the ground that even after the attainment of majority by the defendants till the institution of the suit for over 21 years the said defendants never claimed any title or possession of the suit land as against the plaintiffs concerned. This case is also distinguishable that in the present 12 years had not passed from the attainment of majority by the defendants till the institution of the suit and on that account the aforesaid decision is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case. The decisions referred to in 26 C.W.N. 65, A. I.R. 1940 (Cal) 589 and A. I. R. 1941 (Sind) 50 as mentioned hereinbefore relate to partition suits where it was consistently held that there cannot be any adverse possession against a minor when they were not in a position to assert any claim to any right, title and interest. 

 "The fundamental rule is that in order of establish adverse possession as between co-sharers. there must be evidence of an open assertion of a hostile title by one of them to the knowledge of the others; mere non-participation in the profits by one party and exclusive occupation by the other is not conclusive. Apart from this we have the important circumstances that in this case the rightful owner, the second. plaintiff Ramnibas, who, when a child a few months old was taken in adoption in 1892, was a minor till at least 1910; it is thus difficult to appreciate how the contesting Defendants began to hold adversely to the knowledge of the infant in 1901. Indeed, before this action was brought, there was no attempt on the part of the defendant to rely on adverse possession, their presence was that they were the rightful owners, and one of them, the first Defendant, has pledged his cash in support of that untrue allegation in the witness box in this suit; they cannot consistently urge that from 1901 the first defendant began to hold adversely to the knowledge of the rightful owner. 

 I cannot see how title by adverse possession can originate during the mine thy of the person sought to be defeated by adverse possession. To acquire adverse possession there must acts of exclusion or ouster amounting to open assertion of hostile title, knowledge of which must be attributable to the person sought to be excluded so as to enable him to resist the acts. A minor is not in a position to know of or to resist acts of ouster and I cannot therefore understand how there could be overt acts amounting to open assertion of a hostile title against a minor. 

 12. In view of the aforesaid principle of law laid down in the decision referred to above it can be unmistakably observed that no adverse interest can be claimed against a minor during his minority and it can only be claimed, against such minor when he attains majority. Keeping that principle in view it is quite evident in the present case that from the attainment of majority by the defendants and till the institution of the present suit by the plaintiffs, since 12 years had not elapsed, there was no question of any adverse possession of the suit land by the plaintiffs as against the defendants. In such circumstances the plaintiffs cannot get a decree with regard to the declaration of title and confirmation of possession of the suit land relating to the shares of contesting defendants Nos. 1 and 6.

parties:
Bangladesh .... Appellant.
Vs.
Babu Indu Bhusan Gupta & others .... Respondents.
full_judgment:
2. The plaintiff respondents brought this suit being Title Suit No. 42 of 1943 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge at Bakerganj for a declaration of title and recovery of khas possession and for mesne profits as well as for a permanent injunction against the Province of Bengal and others. The subject-matter of this litigation is a newly formed char measuring more or less 700 acres thrown up by a tributary of the Meghna at Bhola and the rival claimants are the plaintiffs and the co-plaintiffs who have been subsequently added as such on the one hand, and defendant No.1, which was originally Province of Bengal, subsequently after partition of the country was province of East Bengal, and now after the liberation of the country, Bangladesh. The basis of the claim made by the plaintiffs and the co-plaintiffs is that the disputed char is partly a reformation in situation of their lands of Osat Taluk and Howla in Char Ilsha which appertained to a permanently settled estate and partly accretions thereto. 

 4. The suit was decreed in part on contest against defendant No. 1 and export against the rest on 13.9.47. Of the said decree, the title of the plaintiffs and the co-plaintiffs to the lands of the whole of the dispute char excepting a certain portion was declared and they were also granted a decree for khas possession of the same. The learned Subordinate held, in course of his judgment, of the question of the plaintiff's title, that the southern portion of the Char was definitely a reformation in situ of the plaintiff's land and the northern portion excepting some lands was an accretion thereto. As regards the Government's claim that it was a reformation of the Government land in situ and accretion to the same it was held that as soon as the Char belonging to the Government was diluviated it had become a part of the bed of the river arid lapsed back into the public domain so fully and completely that the lands might be gained from it by gradual accession under clause (1) of section, 4 of the Alluvion and Diluvion Regulation (Regulation XI of 1825). 

 5. The Province of East Bengal preferred an appeal against the said decree to the Dacca High Court being F A. No. 52 of 1948. This appeal was heard by a Division Branch of the said Court, (Murshed and Idris Ji), who, by their judgment dated 14-7-1960, allowed the appeal in part, holding that Char Ananda part III which was a Govt. Estate having reformed in the old site, the Government could claim by virtue of its title as the original owner and as such the fight of accretion could not be claimed by the plaintiffs in respect of such lands,. The learned Judges disposed of the appeal by the following orders: 

 13. Learned Attorney-General has next contended that the learned Subordinate Judge misconstrued the order of remand and failed to notice that the contention of the Government was that the plaintiffs cannot claim any title in respect of the land of Char Ananda Part III as well as the accretions thereto and that the decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge was bad because in declaring title in favor of the Government in respect of the lands of Char Ananda Part III the accretions to the said Char were not taken in to consideration. 

 15. The next contention of the learned Attorney General has been that on reference to the map of the disputed land as well as of Char Ananda Part III it would be clear that if Char Ananda Part III is excluded from the decretal lands of the plaintiffs, in that case the lands lying to the north of Char Ananda Part III, as has been depicted in the case map, cannot be conceivably claimed by the plaintiff's as accretions to the Char Ilsha claimed by them as reformation in situ, which is lying to the south or south east of Char Ananda Part III, because there is no physical continuity between the lands of the plaintiffs appertaining to Char Ilsha and the lands lying to the north of Char Ananda Part III. It is no doubt true that the plaintiffs have come to the Court for a declaration of their title to the disputed land as reformation of their own lands in their old site as well as accretions to the said lands and if the lands lying to the north of Char Ananda Part III, which are separated from the lands of Chair Ilsha by Char Ananda Part III itself, cannot be claimed as accretions, it is difficult to conceive that such lands having no physical contiguity with Char Ilsha can be regards as accretions to the lands of the plaintiffs. It seems to us, however, that it is not open to this Court to interfere with the said judgment and order of the Dacca High Court even if we are of the view that if Char Ananda Part III is to be excluded from the decree of the plaintiffs on the ground that it was a reformation of the Government lands in situ, the lands lying to the north of the said Char which are completely separated from the lands of the plaintiffs cannot be acquired by the plaintiffs as accretion to their lands. The defendant having preferred no appeal against the judgment of the Dacca High Court they cannot question the validity of the said judgment at this stage and this Court which is of co-ordinate jurisdiction is not, in our opinion, competent to sit in appeal over that. 

 21. In this connection, it may be mentioned that a possible argument may also be made that the High Court was not correct in holding that the Government, just like a private owner of land, was entitled to claim right to alleviated lands as reformation in situ in preference to a private owner's claim of accretion and that the right of accretion to which a private individual was entitled, was not available in respect of the lands which the Government could claim as reformation in situ. This view appears to be clearly opposed to the principle as enunciated by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the case of Felix Lopez Vs. Muddun Mohan Thakoor and others reported in 13 Moore's Indian Appeals 467. The Judicial Committee in interpreting section 4(1) of the Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Regulation (Regulation XI of 1825) laid down the law in the following words: 

 23. The bed of a public navigable river or sea is the property of that State and a private owner of land can exercise the right of accretion in respect of such lands only. A char or an island thrown up in the midst of a public navigable river out of its bed becomes the property of the State, according to third clause of section 4 of the said Regulation if it is separated from the lands of the riparian owners by non-fordable streams. If such a char or island goes under water, it becomes again a part of the bed of the river and lapses back into the public domain. If the land of this bed reappear by a slow and gradual process by the side of the land of a private owner, it is, according to the line of decisions referred to above, a case of acquisition of the right by way of accretion by the said private owner and there is no question of accrual of any Government right on the basis of reformation in situ. None of the cases referred to in the judgment of the Dacca High Court, namely, Lope Vs. Muddun Mohan 13 Moor's Indian Appeals 467, Maharaja Bahadur Keshora Prosad Singh Vs. Secretary of State,  A.I.R. 1927 P.C. 89 same case 54 I.A. 156, same case 31 C.W.N. 717, Rahimuddin Matabbar Vs. Naimuddin Howladar 31 C.W.N. 751 same case  A.I.R. 1927 Cal. 565 and Surendra Lal Depal Vs. Satya Tamas Ghosal, 12 D.L.R. 214 same case P.L.D. 1960 S.C. (Pak.) 179, is an authority for the proposition that the Government can claim title to alleviated lands as reformation in situ in preference to a private claim of title by accretion.

parties:
Sayed Ali alias Syed Ali Sardar ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
1. State, 2, Abdul Jabbar ------ Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
4. The learned Additional Sessions Judge further noticed that the complainant had to purchase the truck without documentary evidence because, the accused had not obtained till then any receipt for title deed on the original owner. The learned appellate Court below further noticed the contention that assuming the truck was in possession of the complainant on the basis of bhara the accused had no right to take it away from the possession of the complainant and approved the finding of the trial Court that the accused took away the truck with dishonest intention and thereby committed an offence under section 379 B.P.C. 

 It is not disputed that this truck originally belonged to P.W. 6. He sold the same to the accused Sayed Ali Sardar. This fact is borne on in Exhibit A the sale receipt that was given by P.W.6 to the accused on 1.6.69. The complainant stated that he purchased on 1.4.69 from the accused. 

 6. Mr. Mozibur Rahman pointedly drew the attention of the Court that section 91 of the Evidence Act precludes any interpretation by oral evidence of Ext. A. If Exhibit A remains unassailed the falsity of the prosecution becomes apparent because the accused could not sell something on 1.4.69 which he acquired on 1.6.69. This argument is of substance. It is to be noted that the complainant set up a prosecution case that he purchased this truck but no evidence was brought on record which would substantiate the claim of the complainant. Exhibit 4 and 5 series showing the purchase or some spare parts for causing some repairs to the truck could not confer an title on the complainant over the truck as contemplated by the Motor Vehicle Act. Section 31 of the Motor Vehicle Act provides that every transfer of ownership of the vehicle has to be reported to the registering authority by the transferor within 14 days of the transfer and by the transferee within 30 days of the transfer Section 2 prohibit the use of the vehicle unless the sale is registered in accordance with Chapter 3. Section 32 appears under chapter 3. Section 112 is the penal section. The position appears to be this without getting the registration within 30 days of the transfer if the transferee drives the vehicle or causes it to be driven he would on complaint to the Magistrate be liable to be prosecuted and punished under section 22 read with section 112 of the Act. One principle of jurisprudence is that one cannot take advantage of one's own wrong. The complainant on his own showing had not acquired any right and title over the vehicle in question and in that view his allegation is that the vehicle was taken away from his possession without his consent is without foundation inasmuch as his possession is not recognizable in law. This finding is alone sufficient to demolish the prosecution case. As the courts below considered the hypothetical case that even assuming the defence version is correct that the truck was given on bhara still the accused had no right to change the nature of the truck remains to be considered. Mr. Rafiqur Rahman could not lay his finger on evidence to show that the truck was given to the complainant for a specified period. Had there been any such evidence an argument of very weak nature could be advanced. Since there is no such evidence this finding of the Coals below was based on conjecture and is liable to be set aside.

lawyer:
Rahima Khatun, Deputy Attorney-General with Rand Amin, Shahla Sharafat Nazad and Farida Parvin, Assistant Attorney-Generals—For the Petitioners.

Government of Bangladesh and others ----- Petitioners
VS
Ahammad Ali and others -------- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
2. Facts relevant for disposal of the Rule, in brief, are that opposite parties 1-5 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 121 of 1999 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Shreepur, Gazipur for declaration of title in the suit land measuring an area of 1.66 acres as described in the schedule to the pliant. In the plaint they stated that Tonai Sheikh, Fazar Ali Sheikh and Ayub Sheikh were the recorded tenants of the suit land. Tonal died leaving his 3 sons Hasen, Hossain and Abdul. Abdul sold out 0.70 acres through a kabala dated 08-1-1955 to plaintiffs 1-3 and handed over possession thereof. Mahar Ali died leaving his father and mother as heirs. Fazar Ali died leaving his only daughter Meherjan who sold her share to Soude Ali and Sujjad Ali. Nayeb Ali died leaving behind his son Nazar Ali who got 2.61 acres as heir and 0.1166 acres from his son Mohar Ali, i.e., in total 2.72 acres. He died leaving behind his wife Monisa Nessa daughter Helena and plaintiffs 1-4 with 6 sons. Ahmed Ali sold out 0.0525 acres on 09-4-1996 to plaintiff 5. Nazar Ali during his life time sold some land to Helena and Monisa on 16-9-1989 and further gifted 0.28 acres to Mirza Ali and Mojibor Rahman through a heba. Shamser Ali sold 0.07 acres through a kabala dated 4-1-1992 to Mojibor and the latter sold the same to plaintiff 3 on 4-10-1994 and handed over possession thereof. Mojibor further gifted 0.14 acres to plaintiffs 3 and 4 on 19-1-1991. Shamser Ali sold 0.105 acres on 5-3-1976 to plaintiff 1 and handed over possession. Helena sold 0.0975 acres on 22-11-1994 to plaintiff 4. SA khatian was correctly prepared in the name of Nazar Ali. The plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land measuring 1.66 acres. They went to pay rent to the tahshil office on 13-10-1999 but the tahshildar refused to accept it showing reason of preparing record in the name of government. The above record of rights clouded the title of the plaintiffs over the suit land. Hence the suit for declaration that RS record prepared in the name of government is erroneous. 

 3. Defendant 2 government contested the suit by filing written statement. They contended that the suit has been filed on false statements, it is bad for defect of parties and not maintainable in the present form. They further stated that CS record was prepared in the name of Tonai Sheikh and others and SA record was prepared in the name of Nayeb Ali and others in respect of khatians 451 and 456. The land of SA khatian 150 was recorded in RS plots 977, 987, 984. 986, 902, 911, 1999. 1022. 1012. 1017, 902 and 903 in the name of the government. The above recent record has been correctly prepared and, as such, the suit would be dismissed. 

 4. The trial Court framed 5 issues to adjudicate the matter in dispute. During trial the plaintiffs examined 4 witnesses and produced their documents as exhibits 1-4 while the defendants government examined 1 but produced no document in support of their claim. However the Assistant Judge, Shreepur, Gazipur by the judgment dated 28-11-2000 decreed the suit declaring plaintiffs' title in the suit land. The Court further declared that RS record prepared in the name of the government is erroneous. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree the defendants preferred appeal before the District Judge, Gazipur bearing Number 85 of 2011 with an application for condonation of delay of 3700 days. Learned District Judge kept the appeal for admission hearing. Subsequently upon hearing he rejected the application for condonation of delay by the judgment and order passed on 16-6-2011 and refused to admit the appeal being barred by limitation. Being aggrieved by the defendant-appellants moved in this Court in a revisional application with an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act for condonation of delay of 3299 days upon which this Rule was issued. 

 5. Ms Rahima Khatun, learned Deputy Attorney-General takes me through the revisional application the application for condonation of delay and the supplementary affidavit filed on 03-6-2024. She then refers to the cases of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Divisional Forest Office); Mymensingh Forest Division vs. Abdur Sobhan and others, 73 DLR (AD) 1; Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Rcingpur vs. Hasrat Mohani and others, 2 (ADC) 715; Khairullah (Md) vs. ADC (Revenue) and another; 54 DLR (AD) 13 and Divisional Forest Offices; Village 12, Mohakhali, Dhaka and another vs Md Abdul Hossen @ Amir Hossen and others, 66 DLR 661 and submits that although the delay in this case is inordinate but in the application for condonation of delay and in the supplementary affidavit sufficient reason for it has been shown. The government has to move through different organs for taking opinion in filing revision and for that reason' delay occurred. In the cited cases our apex Court expressed of taking lenient view in disposing an application filed by the government for condonation of delay. In this case if the facts and circumstances narrated in the application is considered the delay may be condoned to secure the ends of justice. She takes me through the judgment passed by the trial Court and submits that the suit in the present form was not maintainable and, as such, no decree can be passed in it. Admittedly, the suit land has been recorded in the name of the government as khas. In view of the ratio laid in the aforesaid cases, the delay may be condoned giving a chance to the petitioners to hear the appeal on merit. The Rule, therefore, would be made absolute. 

 7. I have considered the submissions of both the sides, the application for condonation of delay the supplementary affidavit, the counter affidavit, the other materials on record and the ratio of the cases cited by the parties. 

 8. It appears that the opposite parties to this Rule instituted the original suit praying for declaration of title and for further declaration that the RS record prepared in name of the government is erroneous. The petitioners government contested the suit by filing written statement and examined a witness on their behalf. However, the trial Court decreed the suit on contest by its judgment and decree passed on 28-11-2000. After long lapse of 3700 days of the period of limitation the defendant government filed an appeal before the District Judge, Gazipur with an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act to condone the delay of 3,700 days. In the application for condonation of delay the appellants had assigned reason only that when the plaintiffs filed application for correction of the record of rights then they came to learn about the judgment and decree passed by the Assistant Judge and, as such, the delay occurred. The District Judge found the explanation offered by the petitioners not satisfactory, rejected the application for condonation of delay and consequently refused to admit the appeal being barred by limitation which has been challenged in the revisional application.

parties:
Meejab Limited repre-sented by its Managing  Director  ........Plaintiff-Appellant
VS
AA Knitspin Limited represented by its Managing Director and others Defendants-Respondents
full_judgment:
3. At the instance of the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 127 of 2021, this appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 9-2-2021 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka, rejecting an application filed by the plaintiff-appellant under Order XXXIX, rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 The appellant as plaintiff originally filed a suit being Title Suit No. 127 of 2021 in the First Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka seeking reliefs, amongst others, for declaration that the plaintiff through the defendant Nos. 10-11 is not bound to make payment to the defendant Nos. 1-5 against the Back-to-Back Letters of Credit (briefly, BTB LC). 

 17. The learned counsel by referring to the Delivery Challans, Truck Receipts, Commercial Invoices, Packing lists, Certificates of Origin, Beneficiary Certificates { Annexure-A, A(I), A(II), A(1II), A(IV), A(V), A(VI), A(VII), B, B(I), B(II), B(III), B(IV), B(V), B(VI), B(V11) and B(VIII) } annexed by the respondent No. 2 with the application for dismissing the appeal also submits that all those documents clearly depict that the plaintiff had duly received the goods supplied by the respondent No. 3 and neither the plaintiff nor the pro forma defendants ever raised any objection or found discrepancies either in regard to the goods supplied or of the shipping documents and, hence, the plaintiff-appellant is not entitled to any ad interim order from any court of law and, as such, the appeal is liable to be dismissed and the rule discharged. 

 "From the above discussion, we come to the conclusion that, with the establishment of a letter of credit a contract is created between the issuing bank and the negotiating bank without creating any right to a stranger. The letter of credit is an independent contract and not qualified by the original contract of sale though it is based on it. It is also not affected by any dispute between the buyer and the seller. The court will not allow interference by outsiders with the letter of credit as it is bound to have serious repercussions on the international trade of a country." 

 35. During the course of hearing, we posed a question to Mr. Imam the learned counsel for the appellant-petitioner, with regard to these settled propositions about not preventing the supplier/exporter from receiving payment in any business transaction originated through LC, thereby, denying any justification for passing any restraint order by any court of law. Mr. Imam in response very candidly acceded to that settled law passed by our Appellate Division which meets its legal limits only in the case of fraud. However, fraud as claimed to have been committed upon the appellant has not been satisfactorily established in the facts and circumstances and we have rejected such claim above. In this regard, we can also profitably rely on the decision to that effect in the case of Smart Apparels (Pvt.) Ltd. vs Hanvit Bank Kuni Bong Branch and others reported in 57 DLR (AD) 194 where it has been propounded as under: 

 36. Last but essentially not the least, we have very meticulously gone through the impugned judgment and order dated 09-2-2021 passed in Title Suit No. 127 of 2021. Though the said order is found to be very scanty recording as no discussion on settled principles of law and settled legal proposition, on the efficacy of the LC, yet the learned Judge has perfectly rejected the application for injunction upholding the legal principle followed in case of passing any prohibitory order on the payment under LCs and, thereby, the decision of the court below is found to have not occasioned any failure of justice.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.160 of 2024
parties:
Sadia Nowsin Sikder. -------- Petitioner.
Vs.
Md. Nehal Sikder and others. -------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Borhanuddin J. This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 28.11.2023 passed by the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No.316 of 2023 connected with Civil Rule No.782 of 2023 disposing of the appeal and the connected Rule with a direction upon the trial Court to dispose o the Title Suit No.78 of 2023 within a period of 6(six) months from the date of receipt of the copy of the judgment and order with a further direction upon the parties to maintain status quo in respect of schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties as passed by the High Court Division vide order dated 29.08.2023 in the connected civil Rule. 

 2. Background of the case is that the respondent no.1 herein as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.78 of 2023 in the Court-of learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka for declaration and partition, contending interalia, that Mrs. Layla Sikdcr, Mother of the plaintiff and defendant no.1, obtained title of the suit schedule 'Ka' land vide registered Sale Deed No.9195 dated 20.12.1972 from the original lessee of the land Wakil Ahmed; City Jorip Khatian No.1234 of the 'Ka' schedule land was correctly published in her name; Plaintiff and defendant no.1 used to stay in the land with their mother; Said land was rented to the Iranian Culture Centre since 01.11.2013 and the centre was there till 2021; Mother of the plaintiff used to reside there with the defendant no.1; Mother of the plaintiff had to undergone glaucoma operation and upon two successive operation in 2010 and 2011, she lost her eye sight; Between 2008-2016 the plaintiff has visited Singapore on numerous occasions for treatment of heart disease; Taking advantage of the ill health of their mother as well as plaintiff, the defendant no.1 managed to procure the deed in question relating to schedule 'Ka' land by practicing fraud; Similarly schedule 'Kha' apartment was also obtained by practicing fraud. After demise of the plaintiffs mother all on a sudden the building of the-schedule 'Ka' land was demolished. 

 3. Then the plaintiff requested the defendant no.1 for partition of the ejmali properties but the defendant no.1 lastly refused to enter into a partition on 03.02.2023 which constrained the plaintiff to file instant suit for declaration of title and partition of the schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties claiming the same as ejmali property and schedule 'Gha' and 'Uma' documents are not binding upon him; Lateron the Trial Court allowed an application for amendment of the plaint and accordingly added schedule 'Kha-1' to 'Kha-5' properties in the sched-ule of the plaint alongwith schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties; Upon filing of the suit, the plaintiff-petitioner filed an application for temporary injunction under. Order 39 Rule 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure; The Trial Court passed an ad-interim order of statu-quo in respect of possession, position and transferring schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties vide order dated 12.04.2023; On 07.05.2023, the defendant entered her appearance and on 28.05.2023 filed a written objection against the application for temporary injunction; On 09.08.2023, a supplementary was also filed by the defendant no.1 to the said written objection; On 28.05.2023, the defendant no.1 filed an application under Rule 5A(3) of Order 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure for vacating the ad-interim order of status-quo which was kept in the record by the Trial Court with an observation that the said order of status-quo has ceased upon filing of the written objection by the defendant-opposite party; On 08.06.2023, the plaintiff filed an application for addition of party stating that proforma respondent no.6, Shanta Holding Limited, as developer hanged a signboard in the schedule 'Ka' property and started construction therein and as such the said developer company is required to be added as defendant no.5 in the suit and accordingly Shanta Holding Limited was added as defendant no.5; The plaintiff on 25.06.2023 filed an application for amendment of the plaint inserting certain new schedules in the plaint describing certain fraudulent activities. The plaintiff also filed an application for amending the application for temporary injunction; Upon hearing, the Trial Court allowed the application for amendment of the plaint and kept the application for amendment of the application for temporary injunction till hearing of the original application; On 22.08.2023, the plaintiff filed an application under Order 39 Rule 7 for local inspection with an application praying not to pass any order till disposal of the application for local inspection; The learned Joint District Judge vide its Order No.14 dated 22.08.2023 disallowed the application dated 25.06.2023 for amendment of the application for temporary injunction and thereby reject the-application for temporary injunction on contest and fixed another date for hearing of the application for local inspection; Challenging the Order No.14 dated 22.08.2023 passed by the learned Join District Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, the plaintiff a appellant preferred F.M.A.T. No.361 of 2023 before the High Court Division and also filed an application for temporary injunction on 28.08.2023 which is numbered as Civil Rule No.782(FM) of 2023; On 29.08.2023, the High Court Division passed an order of status-quo upon the parties in respect of suit schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties; Having came to know about the order of status-quo passed by the High Court Division, the present petitioner alongwith the pro-forma respondent no.6 entered their appearances in the aforesaid civil Rule and filed an application in the First Miscellaneous Appeal No.316 of 2023 seeking permission to continue construction in the suit scheduled 'Ka' land. 

 6. Mr. A. M. Amin Uddin, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the High Court Division erroneously passed the impugned judgment and order without considering that admittedly the, schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties belonged to Mrs. Layla Sikder, mother of the present petitioner and respondent no.1, as a lessee under the Ministry of Housing and Public Works and the RAJUK respectively and said Mrs. Layla Sikder by observing all legal formalities lawfully transferred the leasehold title and ownership of the schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties to her daughter Sadia Nowsin Sikder, the present petitioner, by dint of two separate registered heba deeds and the present petitioner after obtaining necessary permission mutated her name and paying rents and taxes regularly having transferrable right, title and possession over the suit land without any hindrance from anyone else and as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. He also submits that the High Court Division failed to take into consideration that the pro-forma respondent no.6, Shanta Holding Limited, complying all the terms and conditions entered into the registered deed of agreement with the present petitioner for construction of multi-storied building in the schedule 'Ka' property and also obtained an irrevocable general power of attorney from the present petitioner and thereafter also obtained approval from RAJUK for construction and as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. He next submits that the High Court Division failed to take into consideration that the respondent no.1 has no legal right to claim the schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties since the same are not ejmali properties rather those are the leasehold properties belonging to the present lessee who obtained the ownership and title by dint of two separate registered heba deeds after completing all legal formalities and the respondent no.1 miserably failed to provide any material statement or allegation in the plaint that the present petitioner obtained the lease-hold title and possession by practicing fraud as such the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. 

 9. It appears that the respondent no.1 here-in as plaintiff filed the suit for declaration of title and partition claiming that suit schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' properties are ejmali properties and the suit schedule 'Ga-Uma' documents are not binding upon the plaintiff. Admittedly, the suit schedule 'Ka' property belonged to Mrs. Layla Sikder, mother of the petitioner and respondent no.1, who obtained title of the land vide registered sale deed from the original lessee. Plaintiff filed the suit claiming that the present petitioner, defendant no.1 of the suit, managed to procure the heba deed relating schedule 'Ka' land by practicing fraud and similarly obtained schedule 'Kha' apartment by practicing fraud. The respondent no.1-plaintiff filed an application in the suit under Order 39 Rule 1 and 2 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for temporary injunction barring defendant no.1 of the suit from constructing any structure or changing nature and character of the 'Ka' schedule land or transfer suit schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' land till disposal of the suit. The petitioner-defendant no.1 filed written objection denying material averments made in the application and prayed for rejecting the same. The Trial Court upon contested hearing rejected the application for temporary injunction holding that since soon after filing of the suit the defendant-opposite party no.1 as plaintiff filed Title Suit No.503 of 2023 impleading the plaintiff-appellant as defendant therein for partition and the subject matter and remedy sought in the suit and that of the subject matter and remedy sought in the application for temporary injunction are same, so the plaintiff-appellant can contest the said suit by filing a written statement narrating his case and all his grievances can be addressed in the said suit. So, there is no reason to get any ad-interim order in the suit vis-a-vis the defendant-opposite party no.1 has already appointed a developer, defendant no.5, to build apartments on the land of 'Ka' schedule. Thus, the balance of convenience and inconvenience stands not infavour of the plaintiff rather for the dependants. 

 11. It is also well settled that in a suit for partition every co-sharer of an undivided property is entitle to enjoy every inch of land until and unless the same is partitioned through metes and bounds by a competent court except any co-sharer is found to enjoy in specific portion of the undivided land, then an injunction can be granted thereon and since 'Ka' schedule property is now belong to the defendant no.1 and the deed of gift has not yet been declared illegal, so the defendant no.1 has rightly furnished an agreement with the defendant no.5 for constructing apartments thereon.

parties:
Haji Mohammad Kutubul Alam being dead his legal heirs: Md. Shah Alam and others --------- Appellants.
Vs.
Md.Gousuzzaman and others ------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Ms. Nahid Yesmin, learned Advocate for the appellant, submits that the High Court Division has committed error of law in not holding that the authority of the Waqf Administrator described in Sections 33 and 56 of the Waqf Ordinance is very limited to accord permission to transfer immovable property of Waqf Estate and that the Waqf deed itself imposes an embargo that the waqf property should not be transferred. She submits that the Waqf Administrator could not accord permission for transfer of the property of the Waqf Estate in view of spirit of Islamic jurisprudence established to deal with waqf property. She further submits that title of the suit property has been vested in the Almighty Allah after execution and registration of the waqf deed. She submits that no one is entitled to transfer waqf property since such transfer usually damages the waqf property. She further submits that the High Court Division manifestly failed to appreciate that Civil Court’s jurisdiction has not been ousted rather under Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Civil Courts have jurisdiction to try all suits of civil nature and the dispute as raised by the plaintiff in the instant suit is a civil dispute which has been rightly adjudicated by the trial Court because the transfers of Waqf property were, fraudulent, void, malafide and collusive. She, lastly, submits that the High Court Division miserably failed to hold that the Waqf Administrator collusively permitted to transfer more waqf property which was in excess of land sought to be transferred. 

 We are of the view that only Civil Court is empowered to make declaration as prayed for as per provision of section 9 of the code of Civil Procedure. We do not find force in the submission Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali. So far the right to sue is concerned the High Court Division in the case of Hafizuddin Ahmed V. Aslam Mia and another [55 DLR (2003)95] observed that in case of any waste or harm of any such property, not only the Administrator or the Mutwalli but also any stranger to the family of the waqif professing Muslim faith may sue anyone including the Administrator or Mutwalli to rescue or recover the waqf property, which is illegally alienated or transferred. No doubt, it could be said that as the property in a waqf, vests in the Almighty, there must be a concern and, undoubtedly, a moral duty to act in a manner that the object of the waqf is fostered. We are of the view that the aforesaid proposition is correct.  That is, the plaintiff was entitled to file the instant suit. 

 Waqf is an Islamic endowment of property to be held in trust and used for a charitable or religious purpose. The literal meaning of waqf is detention or confinement and prohibition. The origin of word “waqf” comes from Arabic word “al-waqf”, which literary means to stop, to prevent and to suppress. As waqf properties are bestowed upon the Almightly Allah, in the use of a physically tangible entity, a “mutawalli” is appointed by the waqif or by the Waqf Administrator, to manage or administer a waqf. Syed Ameer Ali in “Mohammedan Law” has said, “A waqf is thus interwoven with the entire religious life and social economy of the Mussulmans. “Trusts” in the Mussalman system may for the sake of convenience be divided under three heads, that is, public, quasi- public and private”. He added, “It must be remembered also that a waqf is not a gratuitous transfer of property. It is a transfer to the legal ownership of the Almighty for substantial consideration viz. His reward, which is obtained the moment the waqf is created”. He stated, “the Mohammedan Law owes its origin to a rule laid down by the Prophet of Islam,” and means “tying up of property in the ownership of God the Almighty and the devotion of the profits for the benefit of human beings.” ”As a result of the creation of a waqf, the right of wakif is extinguished and the ownership is transferred to the Almighty”. 

 Supreme Court of Pakistan in C.P. No.522-L, 523-L & 588-L of 2013. Sikander Hayat Khan Jogazai V. Muhammed Hashim etc. has elaborately discussed about origin and subsequent development of waqf and waqf property. It observed, 

 “13. But the Mahommedan law relating to trusts differs fundamentally from the English law. It owes its origin to a rule laid down by the Prophet of Islam; and means "the tying up of property in the ownership of God the Almighty and the devotion of the profits for the benefit of hu man beings." When once it is declared that a particular property is wakf, or any such expression is used as implies wakf, or the tenor of the document shows, … that a dedication to pious or charitable purposes is meant, the right of the wakif is extinguished and the ownership is transferred to the Almighty…………” 

 A Waqf has three distinct features, those are (i) it is perpetual, (ii) inalienable (iii) irrevocable. It is an institution which is close to the heart of the Muslim Community. After execution and registration of the waqf deed, the title of the property, in question, has been vested to the Almighty who is the real owner of the entire Universe, the Mutawalli is essentially a Manager and Administrator of the waqf which vests in Almighty. Since the ownership of the property is transferred to the Almighty Allah from the waqif in the case of waqf, the property can not be taken back from Allah once a property becomes waqf, it will always stay waqf. Waqf Administrator is entrusted with the duty of administering and supervising all waqf properties. Waqf is a permanent dedication of the property for purposes recognized by Muslim Law as pious religious or charitable and the property, having been found as waqf, would always retain its character as a waqf. Transfer of waqf property would not in any manner nullify the earlier dedication of property and will not change its original character or title. The property which is the subject matter of a waqf cannot be alienated since the concept of a waqf, wherein, upon a dedication there is an implied transfer of the property to the Almighty which would in law render any alienation impermissible. We find support of the above view in the case of Sayyed Ali Vs. Andhra Pradesh Wakf Board Hyderabad and others reported in (1998)2 SCC 642.

parties:
Pubali Bank Limited ------- Petitioner [in both the writ petitions]
VS
Additional District Judge, Bankruptcy Court, Dhaka and others ------- Respondents [in the both]
full_judgment:
7. Mr Md Nazmul  Hoque , learned advocate for the petitioner submits that as soon as the learned Judge of the Bankruptcy Court passed the original judgment and orders, he became functus officio and was no more competent to change any material part of the order. In the present case, notices were duly served upon all the defendants, but they did not appear and contest the bankruptcy cases. After passing the judgment and order, one of them appeared with a delayed restoration application, which was rightly rejected. But the learned Judge committed serious mistakes in striking out the names of the defendant number 4 and the heirs of defendant number 3. 

 10. We have considered the submissions of the learned advocate and gone through the record. In the case of Mokbui Hossain Mridha as cited by Mr Hoque, the High Court Division after making the Rule absolute in a civil revision, recalled its judgment and made the Rule absolute on merit. The Appellate Division on a certificated appeal reversed the judgment of the High Court Division holding that after passing the judgment on merit, the High Court Division became functus officio. In the cited case, the original suit was for declaration of title over a piece of land, not for declaration of bankruptcy under the Bankruptcy Act. In the present case, learned Judge of the Bankruptcy Court did not change the ultimate judgment and order declaring the principal borrower a bankrupt, but made correction thereto by deleting the names of the heirs of a deceased guarantor [defendants number 3(1(a)—(Chha)] and that of defendant number 4, which he was legally authorized to do under sections 110 and H1 of the Act, 1997. 

 11. In the case of Emdadul Haque Bhuiyan, as relied on by the learned advocate for the petitioner, the guarantor-defendant filed an application praying for dismissal of the plaint under section 28(b) of the Act, 1997. It means that he had sufficient ability to pay off the loan as a parantor. As he could not prima-facie prove his ability, the application was rejected and the original order of rejection was upheld up to the Appellate Division. The basic question, whether he was liable to be declared a bankrupt was not the issue before the trial court. It was also not argued in the cited case that any provision like section 6(5) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 is not available in the Bankruptcy Act, 1997. In the cited case, if the application was allowed, the principal borrower could also escape the liability of repaying the loan. But in the present case, only the heirs of the guarantor and another guarantor himself were struck out from the plaint and excluded from the gazette, if already published. So, distinction is apparent between the cited cases and the case in hand. 

 12. The purpose of Bankruptcy Act, 1997 and that of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 and the Bank Companies Act, 1991 are quite different. The purpose of Ain, 2003 is realization of loan from the defaulting borrower. The Ain in its section 6(5) clearly speaks of impleading the guarantor as defendant in the suit thereunder. In case of failure of the principal judgment debtor after decreeing an artharin suit, a guarantor-debtor is also liable to repay the money and can be proceeded in an execution case. Whereas, the purpose of Bankruptcy Act is to discourage nonpayment of loan to a bank or an individual, and to curtail some civil and political rights of the citizen, who had taken loan and enjoyed the same, but did not repay its creditor. Although in different laws including the Bank Companies Act, both the defaulting borrower and guarantor against a defaulted loan are defined as debtor, they are not equal in all cases. A guarantor is a person who does not enjoy the loan money, but helps another in taking loan and takes the risk of- being proceeded against, when the original borrower fails to repay. That is the reason the Bankruptcy Act does not include a guarantor in its sections 9 and 10. So the moral and legal status of a guarantor and bonower in the Bankruptcy Act is not the same as in the Artha Rin Adalat Ain and the Bank Companies Act. The harsher law i.e. the Ain, 2003 in its section 34(4) prohibits civil imprisonment of the heirs of a deceased debtor. 

 14. Learned Judge of the Bankruptcy Court in passing the original orders dated 12-5-2004 and 23-5-2.004 had committed mistakes in decreeing the case against the legal heirs and successors of defendant number 3 Kamal Uddin, and also against defendant number 4 Salauddin, who were guarantors against the loan taken by defendant number 2. Sections 110 and I 1 l of the Bankruptcy Act confer authority on a Bankruptcy Court to rectify and correct its own judgment, in excise of which learned Judge of the Bankruptcy Court passed the impugned orders.

parties:
Din Mohammad --------- Appellant
VS
Mofizur Rahman Miah and another ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique, CJ: This civil appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 18-5-20009 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No.271 of 1998 reversing those dated 29-6-1998 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Feni in Title Suit No. 12 of 1997. 

 2. The facts, relating to the appeal, in a nutshell, are that the plaintiff-respondent filed Title Suit No.12 of 1997 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Feni for declaration that the ex-parte decree dated 28-1-1997 in Title Suit No.5 of 1996 was fraudulent and void. Appellant Din Mohammad instituted aforesaid suit against the respondent Mafizur Rahman Mia for a decree of specific performance of contract. No process was served upon this plaintiff. Defendant obtained an ex-parte decree on 18-1-1997 by suppressing the summons. The plaintiff came to know about the ex-parte decree and kabala deed (through Court) from one Joynul Abedin on 8-6-1997. He was an accused of GR No.464 of 1995 and defendant petitioner No.1, who was his neighbor, assured him to take necessary tadbir for him in the said GR case. Thereafter, in collusion with his (defendant-petitioner) maternal cousin Nasir, who was a Mohrar in Criminal Court, he obtained his signatures on vokalatnama and a stamp paper worth of Taka 50 on the plea of swearing affidavit and also on different cartridge papers etc. giving him assurance to get release from custody on bail. Thereafter, it transpired that by manipulating respondent's signatures obtained thereon, the appellant prepared a bainapatra and a vokalatnama. A written statement was also shown to have been submitted by the respondent in Title Suit No. 5 of 1996 admitting the claim. The said bainapatra was fabricated and was not executed by the respondent nor did he submit any written statement. Under the aforesaid circumstances, the plaintiff respondent instituted the instant Title Suit for setting aside the ex-park decree passed in Title Suit No.05 of 1996, which was allegedly obtained against him by suppression of summons and by producing fictitious bainapatra etc. 

 3. Defendant appellant No.1 contested the suit by filing, written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint. His case was that the plaintiff respondent entered into an agreement to sell the suit land to him for a consideration of Taka 2,00,000. Out of which, he received a sum of Taka 18,000 and executed a "bainapatra" in favour of the appellant on 17-4-1996. The plaintiff respondent having refused to execute and register the deed, he instituted Title Suit No.5 of 1996 for specific performance of contract and all the processes were duly issued and served upon the plaintiff respondent who appeared in the suit by filing a vokalatnama and submitted a written statement. But ultimately, he did not contest the suit. As a result, judgment and decree was passed in favour of the defendant appellant. The suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 5. Mr Raziuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, submits that the instant suit was hopelessly barred by limitation and in order to get rid of a point of limitation, the plaintiff has made some false assertion, in such view of the matter, the judgment and decree of the High Court Division is liable to be seaside. He further submits that the trial Court brought the lower Courts record of Title Suit No.5 of 1996 and examined the process server who categorically deposed that the respondent No.1 was not willing to receive the summons of the case for which the process server served the summon by way of hanging with the outer door of the respondent. He, lastly, submits that the High Court Division without appreciation of the evidence on record, erroneously reversed the well reasoned judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

 6. Mr Khair Ezaz Maswood, learned Senior Advocate appearing for the respondent, submits that the High Court Division upon proper appreciation of the evidence on record found that the defendant No.1 obtained ex-parte decree by practising fraud upon the Court and that the notice of Title Suit No. 5 of 1996 was not duly served upon the defendant No.1 (plaintiff of this suit) and that it rightly reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court. 

 7. The plea of the plaintiff respondent was that the appellant obtained ex-parte decree by practising fraud so the same is a nullity but in a given case whether such decree was obtained by fraud or not, is a matter which is to be judged with reference to pleadings and evidence on record. The Courts of law are meant for imparting justice between the parties. No Court can be regarded as powerless to recall its own order if it is convinced that order was wangled through fraud or misrepresentation of such a dimension as would affect the very basis of the claim. It appears from the materials on record that earlier the appellant instituted Title Suit No.5 of 1996 for specific performance of contract on 6-6-1996. The trial Court directed to issue process through the Process server as well as by registered post and fixed 7-7-1996 for return. It further appears from the judgment of the High Court Division that it considered the evidence both oral and documentary came to conclusion that notice upon the defendant of Title Suit No. 5 of 1996, that is, the plaintiff of present suit, was not duly served and decree had been obtained by fraudulent suppression of the summons upon the defendant No.1 of the said suit. 

 8. Since the last Court of facts upon proper appreciation of the evidence of record held that notice upon the defendant No.1 of the said suit was not duly served and plaintiff of the said suit obtained decree by practising fraud upon the Court, we are of the view, that it rightly set-aside the ex-parte decree and directed the trial Court to allow the defendant of the said suit to file written statement upon restoring the Title Suit No.5 of 1996 to its original file and number.

parties:
Masud Parvez and others -------- Petitioners
VS
Md Golam Mostafa and others -------- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why judgment and order dated 11-6-2019 passed by learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Gazipur in Title Appeal No. 72 of 2017 rejecting an application for amendment of the written statement should not be set-aside. 

 2. At the time of issuance of Rule, this Court vide ad interim order dated 7-7-2019 stayed further proceeding of Title Appeal No. 72 of 2017 for a period of 6(six) months which is still in force. 

 3. Facts, relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rule are that, opposite party Nos. 1-7 instituted Title Suit No. 87 of 2015 before 5th Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Gazipur against the present petitioners for declaration of title in respect of 0.30 acre land and another declaration that registered power of attorney deed dated 5-11-2014 being No. 9696 was exclusive, forged and not binding upon the plaintiffs. The case of the plaintiffs, mainly, is that the suit land along with other land belonged to Jabed Ali who died leaving behind four sons to inherit his share. Being owners in possession of said land they transferred the suit land by registered sale deed dated 2-4-1979 being No. 1519 to Foyzur Rahman and thereafter, RS record was published in his name who died leaving behind the plaintiffs and they have got the suit land. Plaintiffs have been owning and possessing the suit land by erecting house and cultivating crops and fish therein. They have mutated the suit land vide Mutation Case No. 566/14-15 dated 25-2-2015 and paying rents. Defendant Nos. 1-2 by creating forged power of attorney dated 5-11-2014 denied the title of the plaintiffs to the suit land and, as such, the suit. 

 4. Defendant Nos.1-4, the petitioners contested the suit by filing written statement on 13-8-2015 stating that the land of CS Khatian No. 24 measuring 1.12 acre was originally belonged to three brothers namely, Doud Ali, Abed Ali and Zabed Ali in equal share and accordingly, CS Khatian was published in their name. The land of CS Khatian Nos. 64 was originally belonged to Doud Ali, Abed Ali, Zabed Ali and Sagorjan Bibi. Then Jabed Ali died unmarried leaving behind other two brothers. During his lifetime, Zabed Ali transferred his entire share to the heirs of his brother Daud Ali and SA record was finally published in the name of heirs of Daud Ali. Daud All while was owning and possessing total 1.1812 acre land of two khatians died leaving behind three sons namely, Biramdi, Danesh and Foyzur Rahman. Danesh died leaving behind two sons namely, Suruj Mia, Momen Mia (defendant No. 3) and two daughters namely, Nilufa Begum (defendant No.4) and Helena Begum. Helena Begum transferred 0.0526 acre land to her brother, Suruj Mia vide registered declaration of heba deed dated 28-8-2007 and after the death of Suruj Mia his son Selim Mia transferred his share to defendant No.3 by registered sale deed No. 5670 dated 12-5-2011. Defendant Nos. 3 and 4 being owners in possession of the suit land along with other land appointed defendant Nos. 1-2 as their attorney vide registered power of attorney deed being No. 9696 dated 5-11-2014 and have been owning and possessing the same through their attorney. The plaintiffs have no right, title or interest in the suit land and, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

 7. Being aggrieved by said judgment and decree the defendant petitioners preferred Title Appeal No. 72 of 2017 before the learned District Judge, Gazipur which was transferred to learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Gazipur for disposal. 

 11. As against the above submissions, Mr Kamruzzaman Bhuiyan, learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite parties submits that after amendment of rule 17 of Order VI of the Code of Civil Procedure by the "Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2012", by introducing new provisions therein, there is no scope to allow amendment of pleadings after commencement of trial unless the Court is of opinion that in spite of due diligence the party could not have raised the matter before the commencement of the trial. Learned Advocate further submits that in the instant case trial of the suit has concluded and the appeal is pending and the defendants could not state anything in the application whether in spite due diligence they could not have raised the matter before commencement of trial. Learned Advocate further submits that under order VI rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure amendment can be made only for the purpose of determination of real question in controversy between the parties and in the instant case the question was whether the plaintiffs have acquired title in the suit property by sale deed dated 2-4-1979 which, upon evidence, has been resolved by the trial Court on contest' against the defendants and, as such, there was no issue left to be resolved by the appellate Court. Learned Advocate also submits that by proposed amendment the defendants have deviated from their original defense plea in respect of their acquisition of title and sought to include some persons in the suit who have inherited some portion of land from the suit plots from original owner, Jabed Ali as well as by proposed amendment they have challenged the genuineness of sale deed dated 2-4-1979 being No. 1519, which the trial Court has found as genuine. Learned Advocate finally submits that the application for amendment was filed only for delaying disposal of the appeal and, as such, the Court of appeal rightly rejected the application and thus committed no illegality. 

 13. It appears that the present petitioners as defendants contested the suit by filing written statements, denied the title deed of the plaintiffs and claimed their title to the suit land by inheritance and purchase and in their written statements, they have categorically stated genealogy of their title and adduced evidence in support of their case. 

 14. The main issue before the trial Court was whether the plaintiffs have acquired title to and possession in the suit land by sale deed dated 2-4-1979. To establish their claim, the plaintiffs along with other documents have produced the certified copy of registered deed of sale dated 2-4-1979 being No. 1519 which was marked as Exhibit-4. The defendants, by challenging genuineness of said deed, cross-examined the PWs and also adduced evidence on this point and the trial Court, upon consideration of the materials on record, disbelieved the plea of the defendants and decreed the suit, considering the deed of 1979 as genuine. But by proposed amendment, the defendants have sought to introduce the fact that sale deed dated 2-4-1979 was forged, collusive and not binding upon the defendants which is misconceived one. 

 15. By proposed amendment, the defendants have also sought to introduce a new genealogy of some persons in regards acquisition of their title to some portion of land from the suit plots.
